mechanism: CoT may provide a longer, more inspectable intermediate trace that gives the refiner actionable error targets; this should help methods with explicit critique/proposal stages, while intrinsic self-correction may still drift or over-edit.
predictions: CoT-seeded ProCo beats answer-only ProCo on GSM8K.
CoT-seeded intrinsic self-correction shows smaller or negative gains.
minimal_test: Run GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 and GPT-4 on GSM8K and MultiArith with three conditions: (1) direct answer baseline, (2) ProCo/self-refine starting from a direct-answer draft, (3) identical ProCo/self-refine pipeline but the initial draft is forced to be zero-shot CoT ('think step by step, then answer'). Compare exact match/accuracy and average tokens per solved item; baseline is condition 2, main metric is exact match on GSM8K and accuracy on MultiArith.

scope_conditions.method: CoT-seeded self-refine with explicit critique/revision, not oracle feedback
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step arithmetic and compositional reasoning

evidence_gap: No direct experiment isolates whether CoT traces help the downstream refinement stage itself versus merely helping the first-pass answer.

hypothesis: Transferring self-refine's critique-and-revise loop onto tasks where CoT is inconsistent will selectively rescue hard multi-step cases with many reasoning operations, while hurting easy or format-sensitive cases.
mechanism: Revision should matter when the initial CoT exposes multiple interacting subgoals or operation chains, but extra turns can amplify verbosity and formatting failures on simpler or structure-constrained items.
predictions: Largest gains appear on 3-4 operation examples in FB15k-237.
Reading/XML-style subsets lose accuracy after extra revise turns.
minimal_test: Take GPT-3.5-turbo on FB15k-237 and PrimeKG logical-reasoning subsets plus Qwen2-7B-Instruct on StrucText-Eval. Compare four prompts: direct answer, CoT, self-refine without CoT, and CoT followed by one critique-and-revise turn. Stratify FB15k-237/PrimeKG by reasoning operation variety and StrucText-Eval by structure type (XML/Tree vs others). Baselines are direct answer and CoT; metrics are Precision@10 for FB15k-237/PrimeKG and accuracy for StrucText-Eval.

scope_conditions.method: single-turn self-refine layered on top of CoT
scope_conditions.task: operation-rich logical reasoning versus format-sensitive structured-text reasoning

evidence_gap: There is no head-to-head test of whether refinement moderates the known CoT heterogeneity by operation count and structural format.

hypothesis: Using compressed or length-controlled chain-of-thought as the editable object in self-refine will outperform free-form long rationales, especially for multimodal reasoning models that suffer from verbose CoT instability.
mechanism: Several CoT results suggest useful reasoning depends more on scaffold length/coverage than literal factual detail; constraining rationale length could preserve decomposition benefits while reducing hallucination, safeguard triggers, and refinement drift across turns.
predictions: Length-capped CoT+self-refine beats free-form CoT+self-refine on RealWorldQA.
Refinement-turn degradation is smaller with compressed traces on MathVista.
minimal_test: On RealWorldQA and MathVista with MiniCPM-Llama3-V2.5 or InternVL2-8B, evaluate five conditions: direct answer, free-form CoT, compressed CoT (exactly 3 numbered steps, <=20 tokens each), free-form CoT plus one self-refine turn, and compressed CoT plus one self-refine turn. Use the same final-answer extractor across conditions. Baselines are free-form CoT and direct answer; metrics are accuracy, response-format failure rate, and mean output tokens.

scope_conditions.method: length-controlled CoT used as refinement substrate in multimodal self-refine
scope_conditions.task: vision-language multi-step reasoning with small-to-mid-size MLLMs

evidence_gap: Missing evidence on whether the object being refined should be a long rationale or a compressed reasoning scaffold, particularly in multimodal self-correction settings.

hypothesis: Applying answer-vs-reasoning-path evaluation protocols from multi-step reasoning benchmarks to RAG systems will reveal that some reported RAG gains come from retrieval-supported answer shortcutting rather than faithful multi-step reasoning.
mechanism: Reasoning-focused evaluation methods that separately score final answer correctness and intermediate-step validity can expose cases where retrieved snippets let the model jump to the answer, consistent with concerns about bypassing reasoning paths and false-positive chains.
predictions: RAG answer accuracy will exceed trace-faithfulness by >10 points on StrategyQA.
Noise-added retrieval will hurt trace-faithfulness more than final-answer accuracy.
minimal_test: Run StrategyQA with a strong base LLM under three conditions: closed-book CoT, standard BM25+dense RAG, and RARE-style retrieval augmentation. For 300 dev questions, collect final answers and chain-of-thought rationales, then manually label each rationale for step validity using the false-positive-chain protocol from manual reasoning-chain evaluation. Compare exact-match answer accuracy and rationale faithfulness rate across conditions; baseline is closed-book CoT and standard RAG; metrics are EM and percent of valid reasoning chains.

scope_conditions.method: manual evaluation of reasoning chains and answer-vs-reasoning evaluation transferred onto RAG pipelines
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive multi-step reasoning where retrieved passages may contain direct answer clues

evidence_gap: Current RAG reasoning papers largely report final accuracy, while evaluation-method papers document false-positive reasoning without testing retrieval-augmented settings on the same faithfulness criteria.

hypothesis: Transferring compositional difficulty-controlled evaluation from multi-step reasoning benchmarks to RAG will show that RAG helps mainly on retrieval-supported low-to-mid composition depth, but not on the hardest multi-hop compositions where evidence integration itself is the bottleneck.
mechanism: Evaluation methods that stratify by number of reasoning steps or composition layers can isolate whether retrieval improves access to missing facts versus actual multi-step composition; if integration is limiting, gains should vanish as composition depth increases even with relevant documents present.
predictions: RAG gain will be positive on 2-step items but near zero on 4+ step items.
Oracle retrieval will not close the gap on highest-depth subsets.
minimal_test: Construct a depth-stratified evaluation by taking StrategyQA and HotpotQA items and annotating or filtering them into 2-step, 3-step, and 4+-step reasoning subsets using an existing decomposition prompt plus human spot-checking. Evaluate a closed-book LLM, vanilla RAG with Contriever top-5, and MetaRAG or OG-RAG on the same subsets. Baseline is closed-book CoT and vanilla RAG. Metrics are exact match/F1 by depth bucket and delta versus closed-book.

scope_conditions.method: difficulty-stratified benchmark evaluation transferred from evaluation-method papers to RAG systems
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with measurable composition depth and available supporting corpora

evidence_gap: Existing claims show step-count sensitivity in reasoning benchmarks and overall gains for RAG, but do not jointly test whether retrieval benefits persist after controlling for reasoning depth.

hypothesis: Importing perturbation-based evaluation such as masking and distractor sensitivity from reasoning benchmarks into RAG will identify robustness regimes where retrieval quality matters less than the model's ability to ignore semantically plausible but reasoning-irrelevant evidence.
mechanism: Evaluation-method work uses masking or adversarial condition changes to stress latent reasoning; applied to RAG, analogous perturbations on retrieved context should quantify whether systems truly integrate evidence or are overly susceptible to noisy passages, conflicting snippets, and surface cues.
predictions: Adversarially injected distractor passages will cause larger drops for vanilla RAG than for retrieval-filtered variants.
Document influence variance will rise sharply on perturbed contexts for factual QA but only modestly for reasoning traces.
minimal_test: On FRoG and StrategyQA, build a RAG benchmark with three retrieval-context settings: clean top-5, top-5 plus two semantically similar distractors, and top-5 with one contradiction-injecting passage. Evaluate closed-book CoT, vanilla RAG, and a filtered RAG variant such as reranker-based or self-consistency filtered retrieval. Measure answer Accuracy/EM and document influence statistics per generated token using influence analysis; baseline is clean-context vanilla RAG.

scope_conditions.method: masking/distractor perturbation evaluation and influence analysis transferred onto RAG context construction
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning with retrieved text where distractors or conflicting evidence can be programmatically injected

evidence_gap: RAG papers note noise sensitivity and some benefits from retrieval, while evaluation papers show perturbation-induced failures in reasoning, but no standardized perturbation benchmark directly connects these two lines.

hypothesis: Transferring false-positive reasoning-chain evaluation from benchmark studies into prompting comparisons will reveal that some prompting gains on multi-step reasoning are partly explained by higher rates of answer-correct but rationale-incorrect outputs.
mechanism: Prompting methods that force longer or more structured traces can increase the chance of spurious intermediate steps while still landing on the correct final answer, so evaluation that separately scores final-answer correctness and step validity may reorder prompt rankings.
predictions: Hint/step-wise prompts show higher false-positive rates than direct-answer prompts.
Prompt ranking by rationale-validity differs from ranking by final-answer accuracy.
minimal_test: Run GPT-4o and Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on StrategyQA and StrucText-Eval with three prompting conditions: direct-answer baseline, step-wise generation baseline, and w/ Hint prompt. Sample 200 questions per dataset, manually label each generated chain for step validity using the false-positive protocol from manual reasoning-chain evaluation, and report final-answer Accuracy plus false-positive rate among correct answers. Baselines are direct-answer prompting and published step-wise/hint variants; key metric is false-positive rate, with Accuracy as secondary.

scope_conditions.method: manual evaluation of reasoning chains transferred from evaluation-method work to prompting comparisons
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning where prompts elicit explicit rationales

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload applies manual false-positive chain auditing across competing prompting strategies on the same reasoning datasets.

hypothesis: Transferring difficulty-stratified evaluation from multi-step reasoning benchmarks to few-shot prompt construction will improve prompt effectiveness by matching demonstration difficulty to latent reasoning depth rather than using generic exemplars.
mechanism: Evaluation work shows strong performance variation by reasoning depth and subtask difficulty; if demonstrations are selected to mirror those strata, the prompt may better activate task-relevant decomposition without over- or under-scaffolding.
predictions: Difficulty-matched demonstrations outperform random demonstrations on hardest strata.
Hard-example demonstrations help open models more than frontier closed models.
minimal_test: Create difficulty bins on ReasonQA (L2 vs L3) and MCR using an automatic proxy from benchmark annotations or answer-chain length. Evaluate Mistral-7B-Instruct and GPT-4o under 4-shot prompting with three baselines: random example selection, semantic-similarity selection, and difficulty-matched selection using examples from the same difficulty bin. Measure Exact Match on ReasonQA and Accuracy on MCR, reporting results overall and by difficulty stratum.

scope_conditions.method: difficulty-aware few-shot demonstration selection derived from evaluation stratification
scope_conditions.task: few-shot prompted multi-step reasoning with available difficulty labels or proxies

evidence_gap: The payload contains evidence for difficulty effects in evaluation and for demonstration selection in prompting, but not for selecting demonstrations explicitly by benchmark-defined reasoning depth.

hypothesis: Transferring order-sensitive evaluation protocols into prompt design will yield more robust multi-step reasoning prompts by training or selecting prompts whose answers are invariant to reasoning-output order reversals.
mechanism: If a model truly composes the needed reasoning, then prompting it to produce answer-then-logic versus logic-then-answer should preserve the final decision more often; prompts with high order sensitivity may be exploiting unstable heuristics.
predictions: Order-invariant prompt selection improves accuracy over a single fixed prompt.
Questions with larger answer/logic-order disagreement have lower final correctness.
minimal_test: On GSM8K and StrategyQA, evaluate GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B with paired prompts: logic-then-answer, answer-then-logic, and a selected prompt that uses a small calibration split to choose the template with highest order consistency. Compare against standard Chain-of-Thought and direct-answer baselines. Metrics: Accuracy on the test sets and order-disagreement rate between the paired prompts; additionally report accuracy conditioned on agreement vs disagreement.

scope_conditions.method: order-pair consistency evaluation transferred into prompt selection
scope_conditions.task: prompted multi-step reasoning tasks where both answer-first and rationale-first templates are feasible

evidence_gap: The payload notes order-pair comparisons as suitable for reasoning tasks, but does not show order-invariance being used as a prompt-selection criterion on established multi-step reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Applying evaluation-style reasoning-faithfulness checks to multi-agent reasoning will reveal that part of the reported agent accuracy gains come from unfaithful or error-containing intermediate traces, while still identifying agent designs with genuinely improved faithful reasoning.
mechanism: Manual or model-assisted evaluation of intermediate debate/critic traces can separate correct-final-answer cases with flawed internal reasoning from truly valid multi-step solutions; this moderator may explain why agents look strong on answer accuracy yet remain overconfident or brittle.
predictions: Faithfulness rate will be lower than answer accuracy for at least one agent method.
Critic-based agents will have higher faithfulness than single-agent CoT at matched accuracy.
minimal_test: Run MMCTAgent and AgentCOT on 200 sampled questions each from GSM8K and StrategyQA, collect full intermediate traces, and compare against single-agent Chain-of-Thought and self-consistency baselines using GPT-4 or trained annotators for step-level correctness labels; report final-answer Accuracy, trace faithfulness rate, and false-positive rate (correct answer but incorrect trace).

scope_conditions.method: critic/debate/agent frameworks that expose intermediate reasoning traces
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning benchmarks with verifiable intermediate steps such as GSM8K and StrategyQA

evidence_gap: No direct evidence in the payload tests whether agent-generated traces are faithful under the same evaluation protocols used to diagnose false-positive reasoning chains in standard LLM reasoning.

hypothesis: Transferring difficulty-sliced evaluation from reasoning benchmarks to agent systems will show that agent gains are concentrated on medium-complexity multi-step problems, with diminished or negative returns on the hardest slices unless communication topology is adapted.
mechanism: Evaluation benchmarks repeatedly show sharp drops as compositional depth or reasoning format becomes harder; multi-agent systems may help by distributing subproblems, but fixed-round or fixed-topology coordination can saturate and fail on the hardest slices.
predictions: Agent gains over single-agent baselines will peak on medium-difficulty subsets.
On hardest subsets, extra rounds beyond 4 will not recover accuracy and may reduce it.
minimal_test: Take LogiQA, GSM8K, and ReasonQA; partition each dataset into easy/medium/hard bins using gold step count or existing difficulty labels, then evaluate CoPlanner and Group Discussion (3+3) against single-agent CoT and self-consistency baselines; report Accuracy per bin, average token cost, and accuracy-vs-round curves for 1-6 rounds.

scope_conditions.method: multi-agent debate/collaboration with controllable rounds or topology
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning tasks with explicit or derivable difficulty strata

evidence_gap: Agent papers in the payload report aggregate improvements, while evaluation papers emphasize performance cliffs by reasoning depth or format; the cross-over interaction has not been directly tested.

hypothesis: Using evaluation-derived calibration and agreement diagnostics inside agent consensus will improve when agents should defer, continue debating, or abstain, yielding better accuracy-cost tradeoffs than fixed-round agent protocols.
mechanism: Evaluation work highlights disagreement, answer-vs-rationale gaps, and overconfidence; if an agent system uses these signals as stopping or escalation criteria, it may avoid unnecessary rounds on easy items and trigger extra verification only on ambiguous cases.
predictions: Adaptive stopping based on confidence/agreement will cut token cost versus fixed 4-round debate.
Adaptive escalation on low-agreement items will improve accuracy over one-shot consensus.
minimal_test: Implement an adaptive multi-agent debate on GSM8K and MMLU where three agents produce answers plus confidence scores and a lightweight evaluator scores cross-agent agreement; compare fixed 4-round MAD or Group Discussion against an adaptive policy that stops when agreement and calibration thresholds are met and escalates otherwise; report Accuracy, Expected Calibration Error, abstention rate if used, and total token cost.

scope_conditions.method: agent systems with accessible confidence, agreement, or consensus signals
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning datasets where answer correctness is easy to score online, such as GSM8K and MMLU

evidence_gap: The payload contains separate evidence for disagreement-sensitive evaluation and for agent token/round tradeoffs, but no direct test of embedding those diagnostics into agent control policies.

hypothesis: Applying answer-vs-rationale consistency evaluation from language-only multi-step reasoning to multimodal reasoning will reveal that many correct multimodal answers rely on faulty visual reasoning traces, lowering the apparent reliability of current MLLMs.
mechanism: Evaluation protocols that separately score final-answer correctness and intermediate rationale faithfulness can expose false-positive chains when visual perception errors are patched over by priors or guessing.
predictions: Rationale-faithfulness scores will trail answer accuracy by over 10 points on at least one benchmark.
Models with stronger raw accuracy will still exhibit substantial false-positive multimodal chains.
minimal_test: Run GPT-4V and LLaVA-1.5 on PuzzleVQA and CLEVR with chain-of-thought prompting; manually annotate 200 sampled items per dataset for step-level rationale validity using the StrategyQA-style false-positive protocol from manual evaluation of reasoning chains, compare against a final-answer-only baseline, and report answer Accuracy plus false-positive-chain rate.

scope_conditions.method: manual evaluation of reasoning chains transferred from evaluation-method to multimodal chain-of-thought assessment
scope_conditions.task: multimodal puzzle solving and visual reasoning with generated rationales

evidence_gap: No existing direct study in the payload quantifies false-positive reasoning-chain rates for multimodal multi-step reasoning using a manual audit protocol.

hypothesis: Difficulty-stratified evaluation schemes developed for textual multi-step reasoning will expose sharper multimodal scaling failures than aggregate scores, especially on higher-compositional visual reasoning subsets.
mechanism: When multimodal examples are partitioned by number of reasoning hops or concept composition, aggregate leaderboard gains may disappear because improvements concentrate on easy subsets while hard subsets remain near random.
predictions: Performance gaps between easy and hard multimodal subsets will exceed 20 accuracy points.
Some models ranked highly overall will change rank on hard subsets.
minimal_test: Create hop/composition strata for PuzzleVQA and MuCR by labeling items as single-concept vs dual-concept and low-hop vs high-hop; evaluate GPT-4V, LLaVA-Next, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B with the same prompts, use overall Accuracy as baseline reporting, and add per-stratum Accuracy plus rank-correlation between overall and hard-subset rankings.

scope_conditions.method: difficulty-stratified evaluation transferred from evaluation-method benchmark design
scope_conditions.task: multimodal abstract pattern and causal reasoning

evidence_gap: The payload reports subset effects within individual multimodal datasets, but not a transferred standardized difficulty-stratification protocol analogous to textual L2/L3 or Q→A/Q→AR evaluation.

hypothesis: Counterfactual input-perturbation evaluation from textual reasoning benchmarks, when adapted to visual evidence masking, will better distinguish perception bottlenecks from reasoning bottlenecks in multimodal multi-step reasoning systems.
mechanism: If targeted masking of critical visual cues causes larger drops than perturbing textual scaffolds, failures are primarily perceptual; if performance is stable under cue masking but weak overall, bottlenecks are more likely in relational inference.
predictions: Critical-cue masking will cause larger accuracy drops than random-region masking on perception-heavy tasks.
Guided-vision models will be less sensitive to masking than vanilla multimodal prompting.
minimal_test: Adapt the masking-strategies evaluation used on FRoG to visual inputs on PuzzleVQA and MuCR by generating three perturbation conditions: critical-region mask, random-region mask, and text-only description; test GPT-4V with and without guided vision and LLaVA-1.5, compare to unmasked-image baseline, and report Accuracy drop per masking condition.

scope_conditions.method: masking strategies evaluation transferred from evaluation-method to visual counterfactual perturbation
scope_conditions.task: multimodal puzzle solving and causal reasoning

evidence_gap: The payload contains separate evidence for masking in text reasoning and cue sensitivity in multimodal tasks, but no unified transfer experiment applying controlled masking protocols across multimodal reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Using evaluation-derived false-positive reasoning labels as auxiliary fine-tuning targets could improve reasoning faithfulness more reliably than standard answer-only supervised fine-tuning on multi-step reasoning tasks.
mechanism: Manual evaluation signals about incorrect-but-correct-answer chains can regularize the model against shortcut traces, so fine-tuning learns to separate final-answer accuracy from intermediate-step validity.
predictions: Faithfulness rises over answer-only SFT on LogiQA.
Accuracy stays within 1-2 points of the SFT baseline on AQuA.
minimal_test: Take a Llama-3-8B-Instruct base model and create a fine-tuning set by augmenting AQuA and LogiQA chain-of-thought data with binary labels from manual evaluation of whether each reasoning chain is valid or false-positive, following the error framing used in StrategyQA-style manual evaluation. Train (1) answer-only SFT baseline, (2) CoT SFT baseline, and (3) CoT SFT plus an auxiliary classification head or rejection-loss for false-positive chains. Evaluate on AQuA and LogiQA using the same faithfulness metric as the GTA comparison baseline and standard answer Accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: transfer manual evaluation of reasoning-chain validity into auxiliary fine-tuning objectives
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning with chain-of-thought outputs

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload applies manual false-positive reasoning evaluation as a supervision signal during fine-tuning rather than only as post-hoc analysis.

hypothesis: Difficulty strata discovered by evaluation benchmarks for multi-step reasoning can be used as a curriculum for fine-tuning, yielding better robustness on harder reasoning settings than uniform training.
mechanism: Evaluation benchmarks expose systematic hardness dimensions such as more hops, implicit relations, or answer-plus-rationale settings; ordering fine-tuning examples along those strata may improve compositional generalization instead of overfitting to easy patterns.
predictions: Curriculum-tuned models outperform uniform SFT on StepGame 4-hop+ splits.
Curriculum gains are larger on Q→AR-style evaluation than on Q→A.
minimal_test: Use an open model such as Llama-3-8B-Instruct and fine-tune it on StepGame synthetic graph-based data in two conditions: (1) uniform random sampling baseline matching the SFT setup, and (2) curriculum sampling ordered by evaluation-defined difficulty strata inspired by ReasonQA L2→L3 and Q→A→Q→AR transitions, e.g., low-hop to high-hop and answer-only to answer-with-rationale examples. Evaluate on StepGame by hop count and on a held-out college-level reasoning set with both Q→A and Q→AR formats. Compare Accuracy against the uniform SFT baseline.

scope_conditions.method: transfer evaluation-defined hardness strata into curriculum fine-tuning schedules
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with explicit difficulty levels or rationale-required variants

evidence_gap: The payload shows evaluation papers identifying difficulty gaps and fine-tuning papers showing gains, but no direct bridge where benchmark-derived strata drive the fine-tuning schedule.

hypothesis: Evaluation perturbations that reveal brittleness, such as masking or altered representations, can be injected during fine-tuning as consistency constraints to improve out-of-domain reasoning robustness.
mechanism: If models are trained to preserve answers and valid intermediate structure across evaluation-style perturbations, they may rely less on superficial cues and generalize better to unseen reasoning formats.
predictions: Consistency-tuned models improve OOD graph reasoning over GraphSolver's standard tuning.
Perturbation consistency reduces accuracy drop under FRoG masking conditions.
minimal_test: Start from LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and fine-tune on GraphSolver-style graph reasoning data with two training regimes: (1) standard intermediate-step supervision baseline from GraphSolver+, and (2) the same supervision plus perturbation-consistency training where each instance is paired with an evaluation-style transformed version such as masked entities or altered node identifiers, and KL or contrastive consistency is enforced on final answers and selected intermediate states. Evaluate on the four out-of-domain graph reasoning tasks reported for GraphSolver and on FRoG masking settings. Metrics: Accuracy and robustness gap relative to the unperturbed condition.

scope_conditions.method: transfer evaluation perturbation protocols into consistency-based fine-tuning augmentation
scope_conditions.task: reasoning tasks where semantics are preserved under masking, renaming, or representation shifts

evidence_gap: Existing claims show perturbations as evaluation tools and separate fine-tuning gains on graph reasoning, but do not test perturbation-derived consistency objectives during training.

hypothesis: Applying answer-versus-reasoning-path evaluation from evaluation-method work to tool-use agents will reveal that a nontrivial share of tool-assisted successes are unsupported by valid intermediate tool reasoning, reducing apparent gains on multi-step reasoning benchmarks.
mechanism: Tool-use can improve final-answer accuracy through lucky retrieval, compensating tools, or shortcut execution; step-level evaluation should separate genuine decomposition from end-answer correctness, analogous to false-positive reasoning-chain findings.
predictions: Step-validity rates will be lower than final-answer accuracy for tool agents.
Some tool-use gains over CoT will shrink after path-level scoring.
minimal_test: Run GPT-3.5 Turbo with LATM on Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects from arxiv:2305.17126v2, and LLaVA-7B with P2G on SEED from arxiv:2403.19322v2; annotate 100 correct final-answer cases per system for intermediate-step validity using the manual false-positive protocol inspired by StrategyQA; compare against Chain-of-Thought/LLaVA baselines using final Accuracy and false-positive reasoning-chain rate.

scope_conditions.method: manual evaluation of reasoning chains transferred to tool-executed trajectories
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning with external tools where intermediate subquestions, tool calls, or grounding steps are observable

evidence_gap: No cited claim directly measures whether tool-use trajectories contain invalid intermediate reasoning despite correct final answers.

hypothesis: Porting difficulty-stratified evaluation slices from benchmark-centric reasoning evaluation to tool-use will show that tool augmentation helps most on deeper or harder reasoning strata, but not uniformly across all subtypes.
mechanism: Evaluation papers repeatedly show large drops on harder settings such as L3, Q→AR, masking, and dual-concept tasks; tool-use may mainly relieve compositional burden on those strata while offering little benefit on easy cases or failing on the hardest ones.
predictions: Tool-use will yield larger gains on hard subsets than easy subsets.
At least one hard slice will remain below 50% despite tool augmentation.
minimal_test: Evaluate a tool-enabled baseline such as Chain-of-Abstraction or LATM on two stratified reasoning benchmarks: ReasonQA split by L2 vs L3 and PuzzleVQA split by single-concept vs dual-concept; compare against matched no-tool CoT prompting baselines using Exact Match on ReasonQA and Accuracy on PuzzleVQA, and report gain-by-slice rather than only aggregate score.

scope_conditions.method: difficulty-sliced evaluation transferred from evaluation-method literature
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with natural hardness partitions or constructible strata

evidence_gap: Existing tool-use claims report aggregate improvements, but not whether benefits concentrate on the same hard strata emphasized by evaluation-method studies.

hypothesis: Transferring evaluator-driven model ranking from evaluation-method work to tool-use settings will show that the best base model without tools is not always the best tool user, because tool coordination ability is a distinct capability from raw reasoning accuracy.
mechanism: Evaluation studies find ranking reversals when the output format requires explicit reasoning (for example Q→A vs Q→AR); similarly, tool-use introduces planning, call selection, and result integration, which may favor models different from those leading standard zero-shot benchmarks.
predictions: Base-model rankings will change after adding the same tool stack.
A smaller model may outperform a larger one in tool-use despite trailing on no-tool accuracy.
minimal_test: Using the fixed GPT-4-generated tool setup from arxiv:2305.17126v2, evaluate at least four tool-user models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, text-davinci-002, davinci, curie) on Logical Deduction and Schedule Meeting, and also evaluate the same models without tools under Chain-of-Thought; compare rank correlations between no-tool Accuracy and tool-use Accuracy, with CoT as the baseline condition and Kendall tau as the ranking metric plus task Accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: cross-model ranking analysis from evaluation-method transferred to tool-use pipelines
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning with a fixed shared tool so only the tool-user model varies

evidence_gap: The cited tool-use comparison shows varied performance with a shared tool, but no explicit test asks whether standard no-tool leaderboards predict tool-use leaderboards.

hypothesis: Using evaluation-derived chain-verification signals as the rollout reward inside search-based reasoning could reduce false-positive trajectories while improving final-answer accuracy on multi-step reasoning benchmarks.
mechanism: Manual and benchmark evaluation methods expose latent reasoning errors even when answers are correct; converting those signals into a step- or trajectory-level reward may steer reward-guided search away from superficially plausible but invalid branches.
predictions: False-positive chain rate drops versus vanilla search.
Accuracy gains are largest on answer-rationale settings.
minimal_test: Train a verifier/reward model on StrategyQA chains using the manual-evaluation protocol implied by arxiv:2404.05221v2#c06, then plug that verifier into reward-guided search on StrategyQA as the search score. Compare against direct decoding and the original reward-guided search baseline from arxiv:2404.05221v2#c01. Report final-answer Accuracy and manually audited false-positive chain rate on 100 sampled outputs.

scope_conditions.method: evaluation-derived verifier transferred into reward-guided search
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning with explicit chain generation, especially StrategyQA-style answer-plus-rationale settings

evidence_gap: No direct evidence here shows that evaluation labels for chain validity can serve as a stable search reward without over-penalizing creative but correct reasoning paths.

hypothesis: Difficulty stratification from evaluation benchmarks can be used to allocate adaptive search breadth and depth, yielding better token-efficiency than fixed search policies on multi-step reasoning.
mechanism: Evaluation papers reveal predictable failure modes by subtask difficulty and setting; mapping these difficulty cues to search-control policies should spend broad search on hard compositional cases and shallow decoding on easy cases, improving the effectiveness-efficiency trade-off.
predictions: Adaptive breadth beats fixed breadth at equal token budget.
Hard subsets show larger gains than easy subsets.
minimal_test: Build a difficulty predictor from evaluation-side labels on ReasonQA (L2 vs L3) and Q→A vs Q→AR style data, then use it to choose search width/depth in TSE or reward-guided search at inference time. Evaluate on ReasonQA with direct decoding and fixed-width TSE as baselines. Report Exact Match or Accuracy plus average generated tokens per question.

scope_conditions.method: difficulty-aware adaptive search scheduling
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning datasets with annotated or inferable difficulty strata such as ReasonQA-style level splits

hypothesis: Evaluation-style disagreement analysis across candidate rationales can be transferred into search-based candidate selection, so that search chooses consensus-stable reasoning paths rather than only highest-reward ones.

predictions: Consensus-reranked search improves robustness over top-reward selection.
Benefit is larger on compositional relation tasks than on easier items.

scope_conditions.method: consensus-based reranking layered on top of search
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with multiple plausible trajectories, especially compositional relation reasoning

hypothesis: Using evaluation-method style external critique signals as gating feedback inside self-refine will improve multi-step reasoning more reliably than intrinsic self-correction alone.
mechanism: Benchmarks that reveal false-positive chains and answer/rationale mismatches can supply a stop-or-revise signal, reducing the tendency of self-refine to overwrite correct answers with lower-quality revisions.
predictions: Gated self-refine beats vanilla self-refine on HotpotQA EM.
Answer-change rate drops while correctness among changed answers rises.
minimal_test: Implement a 2-round self-refine pipeline on HotpotQA using GPT-4 or a strong open model: baseline A = standard prompting, baseline B = intrinsic self-correction from arxiv:2310.01798v2#c01, test method = self-refine where a separate evaluator scores each draft for answer-support consistency and step validity using a rubric derived from manual evaluation of reasoning chains; only revise when evaluator flags an error. Measure Exact Match and supporting-fact F1, plus answer retention/change statistics.

scope_conditions.method: External evaluator-gated self-refine rather than free-form intrinsic self-correction
scope_conditions.task: Text-only multi-step QA with inspectable reasoning traces

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the payload applies evaluation-derived error detectors as online control signals within self-refine on the same reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Transferring challenge-set evaluation slices from evaluation-method work into self-refine training and testing will reveal that self-refine helps mainly on difficult compositional subsets while hurting easy items through unnecessary edits.
mechanism: Difficulty-targeted evaluation categories such as multi-hop, masked, symbolic, or deeper-level reasoning may expose a non-uniform refinement effect: revision provides value when initial reasoning is under-specified, but adds noise on already-solved examples.
predictions: Self-refine gains are concentrated in hardest slices, not overall average.
Easy-slice accuracy decreases after extra refinement turns.
minimal_test: Take a self-refine instruction-tuned Llama-2-7B or 13B model and evaluate it versus its instruction-tuned baseline on GSM8K and StrategyQA, but stratify test items by automatically constructed difficulty slices inspired by evaluation-method papers: number of reasoning steps, distractor/masking variants, and symbolic vs factual subtypes. Baselines = instruction-tuned and vanilla self-refine without slice-aware tuning. Metrics = overall accuracy plus per-slice accuracy and calibration of revise/not-revise decisions.

scope_conditions.method: Slice-aware evaluation and optionally slice-balanced self-refine fine-tuning
scope_conditions.task: Multi-step reasoning with heterogeneous difficulty structure

evidence_gap: The claims report average gains or failures, but not whether self-refine effects change systematically across evaluation slices imported from dedicated reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Evaluator-ranked candidate selection from multiple self-refine trajectories will outperform single-trajectory self-refine on multi-step reasoning tasks where model disagreement is high.
mechanism: Evaluation-method findings of large disagreement and weak raw accuracy suggest that one refinement path is brittle; generating several independent refinements and selecting via an external evaluator can convert diversity into better final decisions without trusting any single self-correction chain.
predictions: Best-of-N evaluator-ranked refinement beats single-path refinement on MCR accuracy.
Performance variance across random seeds or temperatures decreases.
minimal_test: On the MCR composition relation reasoning dataset, compare four systems with GPT-4 or Qwen2.5-72B: (1) standard prompting, (2) single-path intrinsic self-refine, (3) N=5 self-refine trajectories with majority vote, and (4) N=5 self-refine trajectories ranked by an external evaluator trained or prompted to score logical consistency and answer-question alignment. Report Accuracy as primary metric, plus run-to-run standard deviation over 5 decoding seeds/temperatures as stability metric.

scope_conditions.method: Multi-trajectory self-refine with evaluator-based selection
scope_conditions.task: Reasoning tasks that permit multiple candidate chains and a final discrete answer

evidence_gap: The payload includes disagreement analyses and self-refine instability, but no direct test of evaluator-ranked selection over multiple refinement trajectories on these reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Applying RAG-style noise-aware evidence filtering to few-shot prompting could improve multi-step reasoning accuracy by selecting only demonstrations whose intermediate facts do not conflict with the model’s likely internal answer path.
mechanism: RAG findings suggest gains disappear when filtering noise costs exceed utility, so a prompt-side analogue may work by pruning misleading in-context examples and retaining only support that aligns with latent reasoning states rather than raw semantic similarity.
predictions: Conflict-pruned demos beat similarity-only demo selection.
Benefits are larger on logical reasoning than on easy retrieval-free tasks.
minimal_test: Implement a demonstration selector for GSM8K and StrategyQA that first retrieves 8 candidate exemplars by embedding similarity, then removes candidates whose generated rationale or final answer conflicts with a verifier model’s predicted subgoal sequence for the query; compare against 0-shot CoT, random 4-shot, embedding-similarity 4-shot, and GraphIC-style example retrieval prompting; use GPT-4o-mini or Llama-3-8B-Instruct, report exact-match accuracy and average prompt tokens.

scope_conditions.method: few-shot prompting with conflict-aware demonstration filtering
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning where exemplar rationales can be checked for agreement with query subgoals

evidence_gap: No direct study in the provided claims tests whether RAG-style noise/conflict filtering transfers from retrieved documents to in-context demonstrations for reasoning prompts.

hypothesis: Applying layer- or step-targeted retrieval ideas from RAG to prompting could improve prompt-only reasoning by supplying stage-specific hints instead of a single monolithic chain-of-thought instruction.
mechanism: If RAG helps by retrieving information for a particular layer of the reasoning process, prompting may benefit from decomposing inference into explicit stages and attaching a small hint or exemplar to each stage, reducing bypass behavior and false-positive chains caused by overly broad prompts.
predictions: Stage-specific hints outperform a single global CoT prompt.
They reduce rationale-answer inconsistency relative to standard prompting.
minimal_test: On ProntoQA or StrategyQA, build a 3-stage prompt pipeline (fact extraction, intermediate inference, final decision) where each stage receives one automatically selected hint sentence from a bank of annotated exemplars; compare against direct answer prompting, standard CoT, and Meta-Reasoning Prompting; use GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2-7B-Instruct; report answer accuracy plus rationale consistency measured by whether the final answer is entailed by the model’s own intermediate outputs under an NLI checker.

scope_conditions.method: stage-conditioned prompting with per-step hint injection
scope_conditions.task: reasoning tasks that can be decomposed into a small fixed number of interpretable steps

evidence_gap: The claims support step-aware retrieval in RAG and hint/meta-reasoning in prompting separately, but not their combination as stage-specific prompt conditioning without external document retrieval.

hypothesis: Compressing retrieved evidence into pseudo-code or graph-structured prompt artifacts before generation could transfer RAG’s context-efficiency benefits to prompt-based multi-step reasoning and outperform raw-text retrieval or raw-text prompting alone.
mechanism: RAG work indicates shorter, more structured context can preserve reasoning signal, while prompting work shows pseudo-code and graph-based representations improve reasoning; combining them may reduce token noise and force explicit state transitions that are easier for the model to execute.
predictions: Structured evidence prompts use fewer tokens than raw retrieved passages.
Pseudo-code evidence yields higher exact match on graph reasoning than text evidence.
minimal_test: On graph reasoning benchmarks used for shortest path and connected components, retrieve supporting graph facts from a graph store, then compare four inference conditions with GPT-3.5 or Mixtral: raw-text prompt only, raw-text RAG, retrieved evidence compressed into pseudo-code adjacency/operations, and retrieved evidence compressed into a small graph schema prompt; baseline against Pseudo+1-shot prompting and GraphLLM-style retrieval formatting; report exact-match accuracy and total context tokens.

scope_conditions.method: retrieval-to-structure compilation for prompting
scope_conditions.task: graph or symbolic multi-step reasoning where evidence can be losslessly serialized as pseudo-code or graph primitives

evidence_gap: Provided claims separately show context reduction in RAG and gains from pseudo-code/graph prompting, but do not test converting retrieved evidence into structured prompt artifacts as the transfer mechanism.

hypothesis: Applying RAG-style relevance filtering and lightweight evidence selection to multi-agent reasoning will improve agent accuracy and reduce token cost by preventing agents from debating over noisy context.
mechanism: RAG results suggest reasoning gains depend on whether useful evidence can be isolated from distractors; injecting a retrieval gate before each agent turn should shrink the working context and reduce error propagation from irrelevant observations.
predictions: Top-k evidence gating lowers token cost versus ungated debate.
Accuracy gains disappear when retrieved snippets are heavily noisy.
minimal_test: Implement a retrieval-gated version of Group Discussion (agent) on GSM8K using a BM25 or Contriever retriever over a corpus built from the training rationales plus external math word-problem exemplars; before each agent round, retrieve top-3 snippets conditioned on the current subproblem and pass only those snippets to the speaking agents. Compare against vanilla Group Discussion without retrieval and single-agent CoT. Measure answer accuracy and total prompt/completion tokens.

scope_conditions.method: retrieval gating transferred from RAG pipelines to multi-agent Group Discussion or MAD-style debate
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-step reasoning with externally retrievable evidence, especially GSM8K/SVAMP-style problems

evidence_gap: No direct experiment yet shows whether retrieval noise thresholds that govern RAG also govern multi-agent debate efficiency on the same reasoning benchmark.

hypothesis: Transferring agent-style critic-actor or peer-review loops into RAG-based multi-step reasoning will improve factual consistency by forcing explicit verification of retrieved evidence before answer generation.
mechanism: Agent studies indicate iterative critique changes downstream actions reliably; if a critic checks whether retrieved passages support each reasoning step, the generator may be less likely to shortcut from retrieval to unsupported answers or be misled by conflicting evidence.
predictions: Critic-verified RAG reduces unsupported final answers.
Benefit is largest on examples with conflicting retrieved passages.
minimal_test: Augment a standard RAG baseline on StrategyQA with a two-role loop: generator produces stepwise answer from top-5 retrieved passages, critic labels each step as supported/unsupported and requests one revision round if unsupported. Compare against vanilla RAG and CoT-only baselines on StrategyQA. Use exact-match accuracy and a support rate metric computed by manual annotation on a 200-example subset or an automatic passage-attribution checker.

scope_conditions.method: agentic critic-actor verification transferred to single-generator RAG
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive multi-step reasoning where retrieved passages can conflict, such as StrategyQA

evidence_gap: Existing claims separately show RAG shortcutting and agent critique efficacy, but not whether critique specifically neutralizes retrieval-induced reasoning bypass in a controlled benchmark.

hypothesis: RAG substructure retrieval methods developed for graph or table reasoning will improve tool-using agents by giving them compact intermediate state summaries instead of full environment context.
mechanism: RAG methods on structured reasoning report strong performance with sharply reduced context; supplying agents with retrieved subgraphs, rows, or ontology-grounded summaries at each planning step may preserve essential dependencies while avoiding context overload across rounds.
predictions: Substructure retrieval improves EM over full-context multi-agent table QA.
Performance gains increase as table or graph context grows.
minimal_test: Build a retrieval-augmented variant of MACT for complex table question answering on CRT: before each agent action, retrieve top-5 relevant rows/columns plus a schema summary using a dense row retriever, and restrict tool inputs to that compact context. Compare against original MACT with full table access and a single-agent table-CoT baseline. Evaluate Exact Match, latency per example, and input-token count.

scope_conditions.method: structured substructure retrieval from RAG transferred to tool-using multi-agent systems
scope_conditions.task: structured multi-step reasoning over large tables or graphs where context size is the bottleneck

evidence_gap: There is no direct head-to-head test of whether structured retrieval's context-compression advantage survives in multi-agent tool orchestration rather than single-pass RAG reasoning.

hypothesis: Applying noise-aware adaptive retrieval from text RAG to multimodal reasoning could improve image-sequence and causal reasoning by retrieving only step-relevant visual/text evidence instead of exposing the model to all observations at once.
mechanism: A controller that selects evidence per reasoning step may reduce the filtering burden and prevent irrelevant frames or regions from swamping the chain of thought, matching the RAG claim that benefits disappear when noise-filtering cost exceeds retrieval value.
predictions: Adaptive top-k beats full-context on Mementos behavior F1
Gains are larger on MuCR than on object-centric sequence tasks
minimal_test: Implement a multimodal adaptive-retrieval pipeline on Mementos and MuCR using GPT-4V or LLaVA-Next: index frame captions plus CLIP image embeddings, retrieve step-relevant evidence iteratively with a MetaRAG-style selector, compare against (1) no retrieval/full sequence input and (2) fixed top-5 multimodal retrieval; report behavior F1 on Mementos and accuracy on MuCR.

scope_conditions.method: adaptive multimodal retrieval with step-wise top-k selection
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step reasoning where raw visual context is long or noisy, especially image sequences and causal inference

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the payload tests whether RAG-style noise-aware retrieval policies transfer to multimodal reasoning benchmarks with controlled context-length and distractor levels.

hypothesis: Graph-structured retrieval used for text multi-step reasoning could transfer to multimodal spatial and directional reasoning if scenes are converted into explicit object-relation graphs before reasoning.
mechanism: Scene graphs or top-view relation graphs may externalize latent spatial relations, shortening effective context and making path-following or directional composition discrete rather than purely perceptual.
predictions: Scene-graph retrieval improves CDR accuracy over raw-image prompting
Context tokens drop while EM rises on TopViewRS
minimal_test: Build scene graphs from images/maps with detected objects and spatial edges, then run a GraphLLM-style graph retrieval/reasoning module on CDR and TopViewRS; compare against raw-image LLaVA-13B or GPT-4V prompting and against a text-caption-only baseline; report Accuracy on CDR and EM/PM on TopViewRS, plus prompt token count as a context-length measure.

scope_conditions.method: graph-based retrieval and reasoning over scene graphs
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step spatial, map, and directional reasoning where relations among entities are central

evidence_gap: The payload shows graph-RAG gains in text-like graph reasoning and multimodal weaknesses in spatial reasoning, but no paper directly tests graph retrieval over visual scene graphs for these benchmarks.

hypothesis: RAG methods that enforce attribution or provenance constraints could improve multimodal analogical and high-level visual reasoning by forcing each reasoning step to cite specific image regions or retrieved visual descriptors, reducing shortcut answers.
mechanism: Attribution requirements may discourage direct answer bypass and instead align intermediate rationales with concrete evidence, which could help when current models rely on shallow textual abstractions rather than visual cues.
predictions: Evidence-cited rationales outperform free-form CoT on MBARD accuracy
Attribution lowers hallucinated visual justifications on high-level reasoning tasks
minimal_test: Add an OG-RAG-style attribution module to a multimodal reasoner on MBARD and a high-level visual reasoning benchmark from VDLM-mm: retrieve region proposals plus caption snippets, require each rationale step to cite region IDs/snippets, compare against standard multimodal CoT and against retrieval without attribution; report Accuracy on MBARD and task accuracy plus rationale-faithfulness score using region-overlap or human verification on the visual benchmark.

scope_conditions.method: attribution-constrained multimodal retrieval-augmented chain-of-thought
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step reasoning with risk of shortcut answering, especially analogical and high-level visual reasoning

evidence_gap: The payload supports attribution gains in text/fact reasoning and shows multimodal cue-use failures, but lacks direct evidence that provenance constraints improve multimodal reasoning quality or faithfulness.

hypothesis: If layer- or step-targeted retrieval signals from RAG are converted into supervised intermediate-step labels during fine-tuning, fine-tuned models may gain stronger multi-step reasoning accuracy than answer-only SFT while reducing shortcut answering.
mechanism: RAG appears to help by surfacing information aligned to latent reasoning layers, but can also bypass the path and directly expose answers; distilling only the retrieved step-relevant evidence into training targets could teach decomposition without preserving inference-time retrieval noise.
predictions: step-supervised SFT beats answer-only SFT on exact-match
step-supervised SFT shows fewer invalid CoT shortcuts
minimal_test: Use a 7B base model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on StrategyQA and LogiQA. Build training data by running a strong RAG pipeline over each question, then annotate each rationale sentence with the retrieved passage supporting that step; fine-tune two variants: (1) answer-only SFT and (2) step-supervised SFT that predicts intermediate reasoning steps plus answer, using the same number of examples. Baselines: vanilla CoT SFT and inference-time RAG without fine-tuning. Metrics: answer accuracy on StrategyQA and LogiQA, plus rationale faithfulness using a supported-step rate measured by entailment against held-out evidence passages.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with distilled step-evidence supervision derived from RAG traces
scope_conditions.task: text multi-step reasoning where supporting evidence can be aligned to individual reasoning steps

evidence_gap: No direct experiment here shows whether RAG's layer-aligned evidence can be distilled into fine-tuning labels that preserve benefits while avoiding answer leakage.

hypothesis: If retrieval is used only to generate conflict-aware hard negatives and distractor documents for fine-tuning, the resulting model may become more robust on multi-step reasoning with conflicting or noisy evidence than standard fine-tuning or standard RAG.
mechanism: Negative RAG findings suggest noise and knowledge conflict can mislead reasoning; using retrieval to mine near-miss and contradictory contexts during training may teach the model to reject plausible but unsupported chains instead of over-trusting retrieved text.
predictions: conflict-aware SFT improves accuracy under distractors
conflict-aware SFT lowers answer flips after adding noisy passages
minimal_test: On AQuA and LogiQA, construct for each training item one gold-support context and 3 retrieved hard negatives using BM25+dense retrieval from a large corpus, including passages that are topically similar but entail the wrong answer. Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with (1) standard CoT SFT, (2) CoT SFT plus conflict-aware negatives where the model must explain why distractors are irrelevant, and compare against inference-time RAG and no-retrieval baselines. Evaluate with accuracy on clean test sets and a robustness metric: accuracy after appending the mined distractors to the prompt.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with retrieval-mined contradictory and near-miss negatives
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive or reading-based multi-step reasoning with realistic distractor evidence

evidence_gap: Existing claims indicate RAG can be harmed by noisy retrieval and that fine-tuning can help with conflicting documents, but there is no direct transfer test where retrieval-mined conflict is repurposed as negative training data for reasoning SFT.

hypothesis: If structure-preserving retrieval formats from successful RAG systems on graph/spatial reasoning are used to synthesize fine-tuning curricula, fine-tuned models may generalize better to longer-hop reasoning than text-only fine-tuning.
mechanism: RAG wins in graph and spatial tasks partly by presenting concise structured context with reduced context length; converting retrieved graph/subgraph or spatial relation snippets into progressively harder synthetic training examples could induce transferable algorithmic priors in fine-tuning.
predictions: structured-data SFT improves high-hop accuracy most
structured-data SFT reduces degradation as context grows
minimal_test: Train Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on StepGame and CLUTRR with three data regimes: (1) text-only SFT on original stories, (2) SFT on synthetic structured traces created from retrieved graph/subgraph representations of the same examples, and (3) inference-time graph-RAG without additional fine-tuning. Use hop-stratified evaluation on StepGame and relation-length splits on CLUTRR. Baselines: text-only SFT and graph-RAG. Metrics: overall accuracy, worst-case high-hop accuracy, and accuracy drop from short to long contexts.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning on synthetic curricula generated from structured retrieval outputs
scope_conditions.task: graph or spatial multi-step reasoning where latent state can be represented as graph fragments or relation chains

evidence_gap: There is no direct evidence that the compact structured representations benefiting RAG can be turned into a fine-tuning curriculum that improves out-of-domain or long-horizon generalization.

hypothesis: Layer- or step-targeted retrieval from RAG could improve multi-step tool-use by selecting only the next-step tool inputs, reducing irrelevant tool calls and raising final reasoning accuracy.
mechanism: RAG findings suggest reasoning benefits when retrieved evidence aligns with a specific reasoning layer, while failures occur when noise-filtering cost exceeds benefit; transferring this to tool-use implies retrieving per-step evidence or arguments before each tool invocation should help if it narrows the action space.
predictions: Step-conditioned retrieval lowers unnecessary tool calls.
Accuracy gains are largest on long-horizon tasks.
minimal_test: Implement a step-conditioned retriever for LATM on Tracking Shuffled Objects (5) and Logical Deduction (5): before each tool call, retrieve top-1 exemplar/tool-spec snippet conditioned on the current subproblem state; compare against vanilla LATM and CoT using GPT-3.5 Turbo; evaluate task Accuracy and average number of tool calls per solved example.

scope_conditions.method: RAG-style step-conditioned retrieval added to a tool-use planner/executor
scope_conditions.task: text multi-step reasoning tasks with explicit intermediate states and reusable tool descriptions

evidence_gap: No direct experiment shows that reasoning-layer retrieval improves tool selection rather than merely adding prompt length, especially on non-visual tool-use benchmarks.

hypothesis: Ontology- or hierarchy-grounded retrieval from RAG could transfer to tool-use by organizing tools and subgoals into a hierarchy, improving tool routing and reliability on complex reasoning problems.
mechanism: RAG work reports gains from ontology-grounded retrieval and graph/hierarchical structuring, while tool-use work claims clear tool hierarchies offload reasoning burden; combining them suggests retrieving from a structured tool ontology may reduce routing ambiguity and hallucinated tool choices.
predictions: Hierarchical tool retrieval improves routing precision.
Reliability improves more than raw answer accuracy on complex tasks.
minimal_test: Build a small ontology over tools/subtools for a LATM-style agent on Schedule Meeting and Chinese Remainder Theorem from the LATM benchmark, then compare ontology-grounded tool retrieval versus flat tool descriptions versus standard LATM; use GPT-3.5 Turbo as the tool user; measure Accuracy, tool-selection F1 against gold/annotated optimal tool categories, and invalid-tool-call rate.

scope_conditions.method: ontology-grounded retrieval over tool metadata and subgoal labels
scope_conditions.task: multi-step tool-use where tools have overlapping functions and can be arranged hierarchically

evidence_gap: Existing tool-use papers argue for hierarchy, but there is little direct evidence that retrieval over a formal tool ontology outperforms flat prompting for multi-step reasoning.

hypothesis: Noise-aware retrieval controls from RAG could transfer to tool-use by gating when external tools are invoked, preventing cases where tool outputs bypass or disrupt reasoning and thereby improving robustness.
mechanism: RAG literature includes both strong gains and warnings that irrelevant or conflicting retrieved content can mislead reasoning or shortcut it; applied to tool-use, a learned or prompted gate that abstains from tool calls when expected utility is low may outperform always-use-tool policies.
predictions: A gated agent beats always-call tools on hard subsets.
Robustness gains appear as fewer confidently wrong answers.
minimal_test: Add a utility gate to a P2G-style or LATM-style agent that predicts whether to call a tool using the current question plus model confidence; on SEED hard questions for P2G or Logical Deduction hard cases for LATM, compare gated tool-use against always-call-tool and no-tool baselines; report Accuracy, calibration-aware Brier score on final answers, and proportion of wrong answers accompanied by tool calls.

scope_conditions.method: RAG-inspired abstention/gating before tool invocation
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning settings where tool outputs can conflict with internal knowledge or introduce distractors

evidence_gap: Tool-use studies report failure cases, but there is not yet direct evidence that retrieval-style noise gating is the right intervention rather than better tools or better decomposition.

hypothesis: Applying context-compression and structure-aware retrieval from multi-step-reasoning RAG to multi-hop-QA will improve answer F1 by reducing distractor evidence without losing hop coverage.
mechanism: Reasoning-oriented RAG methods that encode structure or layer-specific evidence may preserve only the minimal subgraph or rationale needed for each hop, lowering noise load that otherwise harms multi-hop QA.
predictions: Lower prompt tokens at matched Recall@15 on HotpotQA
Higher F1 than chunk-based RAG on MuSiQue
minimal_test: Implement a GraphLLM-style structure-compressed retriever for multi-hop-QA by converting retrieved HotpotQA and MuSiQue evidence paragraphs into a question-conditioned evidence tree/subgraph before generation; compare against standard BM25+DPR chunk RAG and RAG with tree context as baselines; evaluate Answer F1, EM, Recall@15, and average prompt tokens using the same reader model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct).

scope_conditions.method: structure-aware context compression within RAG
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-hop-QA where evidence can be organized into graph/tree form

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the payload tests reasoning-task context-compression methods on standard multi-hop-QA benchmarks with both quality and token-budget metrics.

hypothesis: Applying meta-level retrieval filtering from multi-step-reasoning RAG to multi-hop-QA will outperform fixed top-k retrieval by dynamically suppressing misleading or redundant evidence chains.
mechanism: A meta-controller can judge whether additional retrieved passages help or hurt each intermediate step, preventing the noise-over-benefit regime identified for reasoning tasks and improving multi-hop evidence selection.
predictions: Adaptive filtering beats fixed top-10 on 2WikiMultihopQA EM
Benefit is larger on StrategyQA than HotpotQA
minimal_test: Take MetaRAG-style meta-selection or reflection-based filtering and insert it between retrieval and reading on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, and StrategyQA; compare against standard RAG with BM25 top-10, BlendFilter, and Adaptive-RAG-style routing baselines using the same backbone model; report EM, F1, supporting-fact recall, and retrieval precision of selected passages.

scope_conditions.method: meta-controller for retrieval acceptance/rejection
scope_conditions.task: multi-hop-QA with heterogeneous evidence quality or distractor-heavy corpora

evidence_gap: The claims show meta-reasoning helps reasoning and filtering helps multi-hop QA separately, but not the direct transfer of reasoning-side meta-filtering policies onto multi-hop-QA datasets.

hypothesis: Applying reasoning-process supervision from multi-step-reasoning RAG to multi-hop-QA will improve robustness by forcing retrieval to align with explicit intermediate hops rather than shortcut answers.
mechanism: If the retriever-reader is trained or prompted to expose layerwise intermediate states, it may avoid answer-bypass behavior and retrieve evidence tied to each hop, especially on datasets where standard RAG underperforms due to shortcutting or incomplete decomposition.
predictions: Higher supporting-fact recall than standard RAG on HotpotQA
Smaller performance drop from HotpotQA to MuSiQue
minimal_test: Build a layerwise/step-supervised RAG prompt for multi-hop-QA that requires the model to emit hop-1 evidence, hop-2 evidence, then answer, using HotpotQA and MuSiQue; compare against standard retrieve-then-read RAG and GenGround baselines with the same retriever and backbone LLM; evaluate Answer F1, EM, Supporting Fact F1, and calibration of intermediate evidence correctness by manual scoring on a 200-question subset.

scope_conditions.method: explicit intermediate-hop supervision or prompting in RAG
scope_conditions.task: multi-hop-QA requiring compositional evidence rather than answer lookup shortcuts

evidence_gap: The payload contains mechanism claims about layer retrieval and answer bypass in reasoning, but no direct test that process-supervised retrieval transfers to multi-hop-QA robustness across datasets of different hop difficulty.

hypothesis: Applying RAG-style relevance filtering before each expansion step in search-based multi-step reasoning could improve search accuracy by pruning noisy branches while reducing token use.
mechanism: RAG methods appear to help when retrieved context isolates task-relevant evidence, but hurt when noise-filtering cost dominates; inserting a lightweight retrieval-and-rerank stage at each search node may keep search breadth focused on evidence-supported continuations.
predictions: Node-level retrieval reranking increases final answer accuracy over vanilla TSE.
Retrieved-evidence pruning lowers average tokens per solved example versus unfiltered breadth expansion.
minimal_test: Implement a retrieval-gated TSE variant on StrategyQA: for each partial reasoning state, use a Contriever or bge-base retriever over the StrategyQA evidence corpus or Wikipedia snippets, rerank candidate next-thought expansions by query-evidence relevance, and keep top-3 branches. Compare against vanilla TSE and direct CoT using the same backbone LLM. Report exact-match accuracy, supporting-fact F1, and average generated tokens per question.

scope_conditions.method: search-based decoding with branch expansion and external retrieval gating
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive multi-step reasoning where evidence can be retrieved for intermediate states

evidence_gap: No direct study in the provided claims tests node-level retrieval filtering inside search-based reasoning, especially under matched token budgets.

hypothesis: Transferring ontology- or graph-grounded retrieval from RAG to search-based reasoning could make search trajectories more state-aware and reduce false-positive chains on structured reasoning tasks.
mechanism: Graph/ontology-grounded RAG likely compresses relevant relations into short, high-signal context; if search algorithms expand over retrieved structured subgraphs rather than free-form thoughts alone, they may preserve relational constraints and avoid unsupported hops.
predictions: Graph-grounded search improves exact match over text-only MCTS on graph reasoning tasks.
Structured retrieval reduces false-positive intermediate steps compared with unguided search.
minimal_test: Build a graph-grounded AR-MCTS on the four graph reasoning tasks used by GraphLLM: at each step, retrieve a k-hop neighborhood or ontology-constrained subgraph as the state context, then let AR-MCTS expand actions conditioned on that subgraph. Compare against standard AR-MCTS without retrieval context and against GraphLLM-style retrieval-only prompting. Report Exact Match, intermediate-step validity rate, and average context length.

scope_conditions.method: search-based reasoning with structured retrieval over graphs or ontologies
scope_conditions.task: graph or fact-based multi-step reasoning with explicit relational structure

evidence_gap: The claims show structured RAG and search each help reasoning, but there is no direct evidence for combining graph-grounded retrieval with MCTS-style search on the same benchmark.

hypothesis: Using search-generated reasoning trajectories as supervision for retrieval selection in RAG could transfer search advantages back into retrieval-augmented reasoning, yielding a hybrid system that retrieves evidence aligned to successful intermediate states instead of shortcut answers.
mechanism: Search methods produce diverse intermediate trajectories and better step accuracy, while some RAG setups may bypass reasoning or retrieve misleading facts; training a retriever or retriever policy on successful search states may bias retrieval toward step-supporting evidence rather than answer-correlated snippets.
predictions: Trajectory-trained retrieval improves intermediate-step accuracy over standard dense retrieval in RAG.
The hybrid reduces answer-without-support cases relative to vanilla RAG.
minimal_test: On StrategyQA or HotpotQA, first run TSE or reward-guided search to generate successful reasoning trajectories and intermediate subquestions; train a dense retriever to retrieve passages relevant to each intermediate state, then use this retriever inside a standard RAG pipeline. Compare against vanilla RAG with the same generator and standard Contriever retrieval. Report answer EM/F1, sentence-level support F1, and intermediate-step accuracy judged against gold supporting facts or decompositions.

scope_conditions.method: RAG with retriever training from search-derived trajectories
scope_conditions.task: multi-step QA where gold or silver intermediate supervision can be aligned to evidence

evidence_gap: The provided evidence supports trajectory-based self-improvement and search gains separately, but does not test whether search trajectories can supervise retrieval policies for RAG.

hypothesis: Injecting retrieval-grounded external critique into self-refine will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy over intrinsic self-correction by approximating oracle feedback without requiring labels.
mechanism: RAG can supply step-specific evidence or missing facts that the model uses as an external verifier during refinement, reducing the failure mode where the model merely repeats or rationalizes its first answer.
predictions: Retrieved-critique beats intrinsic self-correction on HotpotQA EM.
Gain is largest when first-pass rationales omit supporting facts.
minimal_test: Implement a two-round self-refine pipeline on HotpotQA and GSM8K with a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or GPT-3.5-class model: round 1 generate answer+reasoning; retrieve top-5 passages from Wikipedia/BM25 using the question plus extracted uncertain steps; round 2 ask the model to critique and revise using only retrieved evidence.
