hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies that help evaluator models, especially LoRA on compact subsets, may transfer to reasoning tasks by preserving base-model general knowledge better than full fine-tuning, thereby mitigating reasoning degradation while retaining gains.
mechanism: Constrained updates can reduce catastrophic overwriting; this may matter more in reasoning where some full fine-tunes hurt general capability, so evaluator-side LoRA successes could translate into a better accuracy-retention frontier for reasoning.
predictions: LoRA loses less MMLU accuracy than full SFT after reasoning tuning
Q-Former/adapter-style sparse updates match full SFT on at least one reasoning benchmark
minimal_test: On a reasoning-capable base model such as Llama-3-8B or InstructBLIP for visual reasoning, fine-tune on GSM8K+LogiQA (text) or MathVerse+MMMU-Pro (vision-language) using three settings: full SFT, standard LoRA on all transformer blocks, and sparse PEFT limited to selected modules analogous to evaluator-side compact tuning. Baselines are base model prompting and full SFT. Metrics: task accuracy on GSM8K/LogiQA or MathVerse/MMMU-Pro plus retention accuracy on MMLU.

scope_conditions.method: PEFT/LoRA versus full fine-tuning under matched data and compute
scope_conditions.task: reasoning tasks where post-tuning retention on general benchmarks can be measured

evidence_gap: The payload shows LoRA benefits in evaluator and visual reasoning contexts separately, but not a direct controlled transfer testing whether evaluator-style compact tuning improves the reasoning-versus-retention tradeoff.

hypothesis: Evaluation fine-tuning that emphasizes structured labeling of evidence or tool decisions could transfer to multi-step reasoning by making intermediate steps more explicitly grounded, improving compositional generalization on unseen reasoning distributions.
mechanism: Tasks like citation labeling, function calling, and tool-use evaluation reward precise alignment between a claim, an operation, and supporting context; injecting the same structured supervision into reasoning traces may force each step to name and justify its source, which could help out-of-domain generalization.
predictions: Improved OOD graph reasoning relative to standard trace SFT
Higher multi-hop accuracy on StepGame when steps are evidence-tagged
minimal_test: Augment GraphSolver+ or StepGame training traces so each intermediate step includes a structured tag for operation type and evidence source, using a formatting scheme borrowed from citation-labeling/function-calling supervision. Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on (i) standard reasoning traces and (ii) evidence-tagged reasoning traces with matched examples. Evaluate on StepGame across hops and on the four out-of-domain graph reasoning tasks from GraphSolver; baseline is standard trace SFT, metrics are answer accuracy and step accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: reasoning-trace fine-tuning with explicit evidence/operation tags
scope_conditions.task: reasoning problems with identifiable supporting facts, tools, or graph edges

evidence_gap: Existing claims report gains from structured evaluation fine-tuning and separate gains from reasoning-step supervision, but not their combination for out-of-domain multi-step reasoning generalization.

hypothesis: If evaluator-style fine-tuning is transferred to factual-QA, training a QA model to explicitly score evidence support before answering may improve exact-match and reduce unsupported answers versus direct answer fine-tuning.
mechanism: Evaluation fine-tuning may teach finer discrimination of support adequacy and error detection, which can act as an internal gating signal before generation in factual-QA.
predictions: Support-scored QA beats direct FT on EM.
Unsupported-answer rate drops at matched recall.
minimal_test: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Inst with LoRA on a two-head setup over Natural Questions Open: one head predicts whether retrieved passages support the gold answer, the other generates the answer from the same passages. Compare against (a) direct QA fine-tuning on the same train split without the support head and (b) prompted Qwen2.5-7B-Inst. Use a fixed Contriever retriever with top-5 passages. Report Exact Match, token-level F1, and citation/support precision measured by whether the predicted answer string is entailed by at least one retrieved passage under an NLI checker.

scope_conditions.method: LoRA fine-tuning with auxiliary evaluator head
scope_conditions.task: retrieval-augmented factual question answering with fixed retrieved passages

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests evaluator-supervision as an auxiliary objective for factual-QA answer generation under matched retrieval.

hypothesis: If rationale-preserving fine-tuning patterns from evaluation are applied to factual-QA, answer quality gains will be concentrated on questions requiring multi-step evidence aggregation, while answer-only fine-tuning may underperform or become less robust.
mechanism: Evaluation tasks that reward step correctness may transfer as structured decomposition skills, helping the model preserve intermediate evidence chains needed for compositional factual answers.
predictions: Multi-hop QA gains exceed single-hop gains.
Removing rationale supervision hurts more than answer-only FT baseline.
minimal_test: Train Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on MuSiQue using supervised fine-tuning with retrieved top-10 passages in two variants: (a) rationale-then-answer targets that require citing intermediate supporting facts, and (b) answer-only targets. Compare both to the untuned prompted model under the same retrieval pipeline. Evaluate on MuSiQue dev with Exact Match and supporting-fact F1; add TriviaQA as a single-hop transfer set to test whether gains are larger on multi-hop than single-hop QA.

scope_conditions.method: supervised fine-tuning with explicit rationale targets
scope_conditions.task: multi-hop factual-QA with retrieved evidence

evidence_gap: The payload shows rationale sensitivity in RAG drafting and step-correctness gains in evaluation, but not a clean transfer test from evaluation-style rationale supervision to factual-QA.

hypothesis: If evaluation fine-tuning is transferred too narrowly into factual-QA, it may improve answer calibration on in-domain benchmarks but degrade broad knowledge performance unless regularized with retrieval or multi-task objectives.
mechanism: Specialized evaluator fine-tuning can overspecialize decision boundaries and suppress general knowledge representations, mirroring capability trade-offs seen in some evaluation-focused fine-tunes; retrieval-grounded multi-tasking may offset this drift.
predictions: In-domain QA accuracy rises while zero-context QA falls.
Multi-task FT reduces the drop versus QA-only FT.
minimal_test: Using Mistral-Nemo-12B-Chat, compare three fine-tuning recipes on TriviaQA with retrieved top-5 passages: (a) QA-only SFT, (b) evaluator-style support-classification SFT on the same examples followed by QA SFT, and (c) joint multi-task SFT combining support classification and answer generation. Use the prompted base model as baseline. Evaluate on TriviaQA EM/F1 for in-domain factual-QA and on MMLU 5-shot accuracy as a broad-capability regression check; also report abstention-calibrated accuracy when the model is allowed to answer 'insufficient evidence'.

scope_conditions.method: single-task versus multi-task fine-tuning with retrieval grounding
scope_conditions.task: factual-QA plus broad general-capability retention

evidence_gap: Existing claims indicate both gains and degradation from fine-tuning, but no matched experiment isolates whether evaluator-style transfer specifically causes a QA/helpfulness versus generality trade-off.

hypothesis: Applying evaluator-style fine-tuning that explicitly supervises correctness judgments and error detection to domain-QA models will improve answer calibration and reduce unsupported answers, especially in high-stakes domains.
mechanism: Evaluation fine-tuning may teach the model to separate answer generation from answer verification, creating internal decision boundaries that suppress confident but unsupported responses before final decoding.
predictions: Higher exact-match with lower unsupported-answer rate on domain QA
Largest gains on legal and medical QA rather than broad WebQSP
minimal_test: Take Llama-3-8B-Instruct and perform two SFT variants for PubMedQA: (1) standard answer-only fine-tuning baseline, and (2) transfer fine-tuning with an added evaluator head/prompt format trained first on correctness-label data from an evaluation task such as function-calling or model-based evaluator examples, then jointly fine-tuned on PubMedQA with answer plus self-verdict targets. Compare against the answer-only SFT baseline on PubMedQA using accuracy and hallucination/unsupported-claim rate judged against gold rationales or retrieved evidence.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with explicit correctness-verdict supervision transferred from evaluation tasks
scope_conditions.task: domain-QA with verifiable evidence, especially PubMedQA or legal relevance QA

evidence_gap: No direct study in the provided graph tests whether evaluator-style supervision transfers into better calibrated domain-QA answering rather than only improving evaluator benchmarks.

hypothesis: LoRA fine-tuning strategies that help small evaluator models outperform prompting may transfer best to retrieval-light domain-QA settings, but provide only marginal gains when retrieval already dominates the pipeline.
mechanism: Parameter-efficient tuning can encode task-specific decision templates cheaply, but its benefit should shrink when external retrieval already resolves most ambiguity, making adaptation most useful for answer selection and reasoning rather than evidence access.
predictions: LoRA beats prompt-only on closed-book domain QA
LoRA adds little over strong GRAG or retrieved WebQSP pipelines
minimal_test: Use Qwen2.5-7B-Inst on two datasets: PubMedQA and WebQSP. Train a LoRA fine-tuned model on each task and compare against (a) prompt-only zero/few-shot baseline and (b) full retrieval-augmented baseline already using GRAG or top-k retrieval. Evaluate PubMedQA with accuracy and WebQSP with Hit@1 and Exact Match. The key transfer test is whether LoRA gains are larger on PubMedQA without retrieval than on WebQSP with GRAG.

scope_conditions.method: LoRA fine-tuning transferred from evaluator-style setups to QA
scope_conditions.task: domain-QA under varying retrieval dependence

evidence_gap: The current claims show LoRA helps evaluators and response generation, and that some retrieval-heavy QA setups have small fine-tuning gains, but no paper directly maps this interaction across domain-QA retrieval regimes.

hypothesis: Synthetic diagnostic data generation methods used to create strong evaluation training sets could transfer to low-resource domain-QA, producing larger gains than ordinary instruction tuning when gold QA labels are scarce.
mechanism: Diagnostic synthetic data can target failure modes and near-miss distinctions, so transferred fine-tuning may improve discrimination on domain-specific questions more efficiently than generic instruction-following data.
predictions: Synthetic diagnostic QA data outperforms same-size generic SFT data
Benefit is strongest in 1% to 5% label regimes
minimal_test: On EconNLI or a medical reasoning QA dataset, create two equal-size synthetic training sets with GPT-4-class generation: one generic answer/rationale SFT set and one diagnostic set modeled after evaluation data generation, containing incorrect candidate answers plus correction labels and brief justifications. Fine-tune the same LLAMA2-chat or Llama-3-8B-Instruct model on each, with a human-labeled low-resource baseline using 1% and 5% of gold data. Evaluate with F1 on EconNLI or accuracy on the medical QA set.

scope_conditions.method: synthetic diagnostic-data fine-tuning transferred from evaluation data generation
scope_conditions.task: low-resource domain-QA and reasoning-heavy classification/QA

evidence_gap: The graph contains separate evidence for diagnostic synthetic data in evaluation and synthetic-data gains in domain QA, but not a direct transfer experiment comparing diagnostic versus generic synthetic QA supervision.

hypothesis: Pseudo-code prompting transferred into agent action planning could improve multi-agent reasoning accuracy by making each agent emit executable-style intermediate plans before debate or critique.
mechanism: Structured pseudo-code may reduce ambiguity in inter-agent communication, so critics can target specific steps and actors can revise more faithfully, extending prompt-side gains from graph reasoning to agent deliberation.
predictions: Pseudo-code agents beat free-form agents on GSM8K accuracy
Critique adoption rate rises above free-form discussion
minimal_test: Implement a variant of AgentCOT where each round requires agents to output numbered pseudo-code actions plus final answer; evaluate on GSM8K and SVAMP using gpt-3.5-turbo or Llama-3-8B. Compare against the original free-form AgentCOT baseline and a standard CoT baseline. Measure answer Accuracy and the fraction of critic suggestions explicitly acted on in the next round.

scope_conditions.method: pseudo-code prompting transferred to agent planning/critique loops
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning with explicit intermediate revisions

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the provided claims tests pseudo-code formatted reasoning inside multi-agent interaction rather than single-prompt reasoning.

hypothesis: Meta-reasoning prompts that first choose a reasoning strategy could transfer to agents by assigning or dynamically switching agent roles, yielding larger gains on mixed-strategy reasoning than fixed-role agent systems.
mechanism: Prompting results suggest benefits when the model explicitly selects among reasoning modes; in agents, this could translate into a controller or role-selection phase that routes subproblems to planner, verifier, calculator, or critic agents instead of using static discussion patterns.
predictions: Dynamic-role agents improve BBH over fixed-role debate
Gains are largest on tasks mixing arithmetic and logic
minimal_test: Add a meta-reasoning controller to CoPlanner or Group Discussion that first predicts a strategy label per question and assigns agent roles accordingly. Run on BBH and LogiQA with LLaMA-3-8B. Compare against the published fixed-role CoPlanner configuration and a no-controller multi-agent debate baseline. Measure Accuracy overall and per BBH task family, plus token cost.

scope_conditions.method: meta-reasoning prompting transferred to dynamic agent role allocation
scope_conditions.task: heterogeneous multi-step reasoning requiring multiple reasoning styles

evidence_gap: The claims show meta-reasoning helps prompting and that agents use multi-round interaction, but there is no cited test of explicit strategy-selection prompts controlling agent role assignment.

hypothesis: Prompt-side diversity ensembles could transfer to agent systems by diversifying initial agent prompts or personas, improving consensus quality over homogeneous multi-agent teams while keeping round count fixed.
mechanism: Prompt diversity may create complementary solution candidates that agents can review and aggregate, reducing correlated failure modes; this is consistent with ensemble gains in prompting and could counter overconfidence in homogeneous peer-review agents.
predictions: Diverse-prompt agents beat identical-prompt agents on AQuA
Calibration improves versus homogeneous peer review
minimal_test: Create a peer-review multi-agent system on GSM8K and AQuA where 4 agents share the same base model but start from 4 distinct prompt templates derived from different reasoning styles; compare with an otherwise identical 4-agent system using one shared prompt template and with single-agent self-consistency. Use gpt-3.5-turbo or Qwen2-7B-Instruct. Measure Accuracy, Expected Calibration Error, and token cost at a fixed 2 review rounds.

scope_conditions.method: diverse prompting transferred to homogeneous-base multi-agent collaboration
scope_conditions.task: consensus-based arithmetic and logical reasoning with fixed compute budget

evidence_gap: Existing claims support prompt diversity and agent collaboration separately, but not whether prompt-template diversity inside agents improves both accuracy and calibration over same-prompt agent teams.

hypothesis: The reported reversal is driven by Accuracy and related metrics: surface-oriented scores reward overlap, so evidence-enriched answers that paraphrase can score lower even when factually correct.
mechanism: Exact Match / F1 treats lexical overlap as ground truth and ignores whether the cited passages actually support the answer, rewarding short confident guesses.
predictions: Re-scoring with evidence-chain F1 or LLM-as-judge reduces the sign flip between claims.
Rankings of prompting variants on StrucText-Eval and related benchmarks shift when switching from Accuracy and related metrics to evidence-chain scoring.
minimal_test: Re-score the same StrucText-Eval and related benchmarks predictions with Accuracy and related metrics and evidence-chain F1; compute rank correlation.
evidence_gap: Few benchmarks report both surface metrics and evidence-chain metrics on the same runs.

hypothesis: An unreported moderator variable drives the conflicting results around prompting on multi-step-reasoning.
mechanism: A confound in data preprocessing, prompt formatting, or decoding parameters correlates with outcome direction and is not held constant across the claims.
predictions: Holding prompt template and decoding fixed shrinks the between-claim variance by >50%.
A covariate analysis reveals prompt/decoding parameters account for the sign flip.
minimal_test: Replay all claims on StrucText-Eval and related benchmarks in a common harness with identical prompts and decoding settings; recompute Accuracy and related metrics deltas.
evidence_gap: Prompt and decoding configurations are inconsistently reported across the claims.

hypothesis: Pseudo-code prompting formats that help multi-step graph reasoning at inference time could transfer into fine-tuning targets as a serialized intermediate representation, improving graph-reasoning fine-tuned models beyond plain natural-language step supervision.
mechanism: A pseudo-code rationale may reduce ambiguity in intermediate reasoning states and give the fine-tuned model a more algorithmic latent plan than free-form chain-of-thought, especially on traversal and path tasks.
predictions: Pseudo-code-supervised SFT beats natural-language-step SFT on DFS and shortest-path accuracy.
The gain is larger on medium/large graphs than on small graphs.
minimal_test: Take the GraphSolver+ training pipeline on the graph reasoning tasks from arxiv:2403.04483v4, but convert each intermediate reasoning trace into pseudo-code style steps modeled after the prompting format in arxiv:2409.17906v1. Train two LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct SFT models: (1) natural-language intermediate-step supervision baseline from GraphSolver+, (2) identical data with pseudo-code intermediate-step supervision. Evaluate on the same small/medium/large graph test sets; baseline is GraphSolver+ natural-language SFT; metric is task accuracy, with a separate report for unseen out-of-domain graph tasks.

scope_conditions.method: pseudo-code intermediate rationale supervision during supervised fine-tuning
scope_conditions.task: graph multi-step reasoning tasks with explicit algorithmic structure

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests whether an inference-time pseudo-code format remains beneficial after being absorbed into weights during fine-tuning.

hypothesis: Meta-reasoning prompts that explicitly choose among reasoning strategies could transfer to fine-tuning as a strategy-selection prefix, improving fine-tuned models on tasks requiring mixed reasoning skills more than standard chain-of-thought supervision.
mechanism: If fine-tuning teaches the model to first classify the problem into a reasoning mode and then solve it, it may reduce strategy mismatch and reproduce the prompting advantage seen on mixed-strategy tasks while avoiding brittle one-size-fits-all traces.
predictions: Strategy-labeled SFT improves average accuracy over plain CoT SFT on mixed-skill benchmarks.
Benefits concentrate on tasks mixing numerical and analogical reasoning rather than single-skill tasks.
minimal_test: Using an open 8B base model such as Llama-3.1-8B, build two supervised fine-tuning datasets on BIG-Bench Hard subsets plus GSM8K-style numerical items and analogical reasoning items: (1) answer plus chain-of-thought baseline, (2) answer plus a meta-reasoning header that selects a strategy label (e.g., deductive, numerical, analogical, symbolic) before the same chain-of-thought. Train both with identical hyperparameters. Compare against the plain CoT SFT baseline on BBH, GSM8K, and an analogical reasoning benchmark using accuracy as the metric.

scope_conditions.method: strategy-selection supervision transferred from meta-reasoning prompting into SFT targets
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks involving heterogeneous reasoning strategies

evidence_gap: The payload shows prompting gains from meta-reasoning and separate fine-tuning gains from explanations, but not a direct transfer where strategy selection itself becomes the supervised fine-tuning object.

hypothesis: Prompt-side demonstration selection and graph-based in-context retrieval could transfer to fine-tuning as curriculum-based example ordering, yielding better reasoning generalization than random-order supervised fine-tuning.
mechanism: Retrieval-selected neighbors may expose local solution manifolds during training, helping the model learn when similar problems require similar decompositions; ordered curricula could also reduce overfitting to superficial formats that hurt unseen tasks.
predictions: Retrieval-ordered SFT outperforms random-order SFT on out-of-domain reasoning tests.
In-domain gains are modest, but generalization gains are larger.
minimal_test: On the GraphSolver training corpus from arxiv:2403.04483v4, construct a k-NN graph over training examples using embedding similarity of problem statements plus task metadata. Fine-tune the same backbone in two settings: (1) standard random-shuffled SFT baseline, (2) curriculum SFT where each minibatch is formed from graph-neighbor clusters and examples are presented with one retrieved similar solved example prepended as a training prefix. Evaluate on the original in-domain graph reasoning test sets and the four unseen out-of-domain graph tasks; baselines are random-order SFT and GraphSolver; metric is accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: retrieval-structured curriculum fine-tuning derived from in-context example selection ideas
scope_conditions.task: reasoning benchmarks where training examples have reusable structural similarity

evidence_gap: The payload contains strong prompting evidence for example selection/retrieval, but no cited fine-tuning study appears to test whether the same structure should organize training rather than inference context.

hypothesis: Pseudo-code prompting transferred into tool-use agents could improve multi-step tool selection and call sequencing by making action plans more executable and less ambiguous than natural-language plans.
mechanism: Pseudo-code externalizes intermediate state transitions and control flow, which may help the model map reasoning steps to tool invocations while reducing free-form planning errors; the benefit should be strongest when the tool API is compositional and deterministic.
predictions: Higher task accuracy than natural-language tool planning
Fewer invalid or redundant tool calls per solved instance
minimal_test: Implement a pseudo-code planner for LATM-style tool use on the reasoning tasks listed in arxiv:2305.17126v2#c01 (Logical Deduction (5), Tracking Shuffled Objects (5), Dyck Language, Word Sorting, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Schedule Meeting) using GPT-3.5 Turbo as tool user and the same tool set as baseline; compare against the original natural-language LATM planner and Chain-of-Thought baseline; report answer Accuracy and average invalid-tool-call rate per example.

scope_conditions.method: pseudo-code prompting transferred from prompting to tool-use planning
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with explicit tool APIs and serial tool calls

evidence_gap: No direct evidence yet shows that pseudo-code prompt structure improves tool-use planning rather than only text-only reasoning outputs.

hypothesis: Meta-reasoning prompts transferred to tool-use could improve when and how an agent decomposes a problem into subquestions, yielding better tool choice than fixed least-to-most decomposition.
mechanism: A meta-reasoning layer can force the agent to first decide the reasoning strategy and decomposition granularity before calling tools, which may avoid brittle fixed decompositions and reduce unnecessary subquestions on mixed-strategy tasks.
predictions: Meta-reasoning tool agents beat fixed least-to-most agents on mixed-strategy tasks
Performance gains are larger on tasks requiring heterogeneous tools
minimal_test: Augment the least-to-most visual reasoning with external tools pipeline from arxiv:2406.19934v2#c02 with an initial Meta-Reasoning Prompting stage that outputs strategy labels and a decomposition plan before any tool call; evaluate on the same visual reasoning dataset used by that pipeline, with the original least-to-most tool agent as baseline and a no-tool CoT baseline; report final task Accuracy and mean number of tool calls per question.

scope_conditions.method: meta-reasoning prompting used as a strategy-selection front-end for tool-use
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning with heterogeneous subproblems and multiple available tools

evidence_gap: Existing prompting evidence supports strategy selection in text reasoning, but not whether that strategic scaffold survives tool-execution feedback loops.

hypothesis: Prompt-side diversity ensembling could transfer to tool-use by running multiple distinct planning prompts over the same tool set and aggregating answers, improving robustness to brittle single-plan failures.
mechanism: Different prompt variants may induce complementary tool-use trajectories; aggregation can recover from individual planner mistakes, especially when some plans fail due to bad decomposition or premature commitment.
predictions: Multi-prompt tool ensembles outperform the best single prompt
Ensembling reduces variance across hard instances with tool failures
minimal_test: Create a 7-prompt ensemble for P2G-style tool-use on SEED and P2GB, where each prompt varies planning style (direct, stepwise, skeptical, verifier-first, tool-first, abstraction-first, concise); use LLaVA 7B + P2G as the base system; compare against the standard single-prompt P2G baseline from arxiv:2403.19322v2#c01 and a self-consistency baseline without prompt variation; report Accuracy on SEED and Percent score on P2GB, plus per-instance agreement rate across prompts.

scope_conditions.method: diverse prompt ensembling over a fixed tool-use backbone
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning where identical tools can support multiple valid planning styles

evidence_gap: There is no direct test of whether prompt diversity yields complementary tool trajectories rather than correlated failures in tool-augmented settings.

hypothesis: Pseudo-code and typed prompting structures from prompting-based multi-step reasoning could improve search-based reasoning by making search nodes more executable and easier to score, especially on graph and math tasks.
mechanism: Structured intermediate states reduce ambiguity in node expansion and allow reward models or heuristics to compare partial solutions more reliably, potentially lowering false-positive branches while preserving breadth-first exploration.
predictions: Pseudo-coded node states raise final accuracy over plain natural-language search.
Benefits are larger at fixed breadth than at increased depth.
minimal_test: Implement AR-MCTS or reward-guided search with two node representations on GSM8K and the graph shortest-path task from arxiv:2408.04648v1: (a) natural-language chain-of-thought states, (b) pseudo-code/typed states inspired by Pseudo+1-shot and TypedThinker. Use the same base model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), same search budget, and compare against direct prompting, vanilla CoT, and the same search algorithm without structured states. Measure answer accuracy and search-tree false-positive branch rate judged by executable consistency checks on intermediate steps.

scope_conditions.method: search-based reasoning with explicit node expansion and scoring
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning tasks whose intermediate states can be represented as pseudo-code, typed slots, or symbolic state updates

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests whether prompt-induced structured reasoning formats improve search node quality rather than one-shot decoding alone.

hypothesis: Demonstration selection and graph-based in-context retrieval from prompting could transfer to search-based reasoning by selecting expansion exemplars or rollout templates conditioned on the current partial trajectory.
mechanism: Instead of searching from a generic proposer, the search policy conditions on retrieved analogous solved subproblems, which may improve branch proposal quality and reduce wasted expansions under limited token budgets.
predictions: Retrieved exemplar-guided expansion improves pass@1 at equal search budget.
Token use per correct solution drops relative to unguided search.
minimal_test: Augment SearChain or TSE on HotpotQA and StrategyQA with a retrieval module that, for each partial reasoning state, fetches the top-3 analogous solved trajectories from a held-out training bank using graph-based similarity over subgoal structure. Compare against the same search method without retrieval guidance, plus direct GraphIC-style prompting without search, using the same backbone model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct). Report Exact Match/Accuracy and average tokens per solved example.

scope_conditions.method: search-based methods that expose partial trajectories and can condition future expansions on retrieved exemplars
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive or decomposable multi-step-reasoning with reusable subgoal patterns

evidence_gap: The payload shows retrieval helps prompting and search helps reasoning, but not whether retrieval should guide search expansions rather than only initial prompting.

hypothesis: Prompt-side diversity and meta-reasoning strategies could transfer to search-based reasoning as diversity-aware proposal ensembles, improving coverage of the thought space while avoiding costly deep backtracking.
mechanism: Different prompt framings induce complementary candidate expansions; using them as parallel proposal policies inside search may increase useful breadth and partially replace expensive backtracking, aligning with claims that breadth matters more than depth and that prompt diversity helps ensembles.
predictions: Multi-prompt proposal search beats single-prompt search at the same node budget.
Accuracy gains are strongest when backtracking is disabled or heavily limited.
minimal_test: Build a diversity-aware version of TSE on MATH and BigBench Hard where each expansion step samples candidate next thoughts from 4 prompt policies: standard CoT, meta-reasoning, re-reading (Re2-style), and hint-style prompting. Keep total node budget fixed and compare against single-prompt TSE, self-consistency without search, and direct Dipper-style prompt ensemble without search using the same model (e.g., GPT-4o-mini or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Evaluate answer accuracy, intermediate-step accuracy if available, and tokens consumed.

scope_conditions.method: search-based decoding with multiple proposal policies under a fixed compute budget
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning tasks where multiple valid decomposition styles exist and scoring can compare heterogeneous partial thoughts

evidence_gap: Existing claims support prompt diversity and meta-reasoning in prompting, and breadth-sensitive gains in search, but there is no direct evidence that diverse prompts should be treated as proposal policies within search.

hypothesis: Pseudo-code prompting from multi-step graph reasoning could improve multi-hop-QA by forcing explicit hop-by-hop operations over evidence and entities rather than free-form chain-of-thought.
mechanism: A pseudo-code scaffold may reduce ambiguity in decomposition by mapping each hop to a discrete operation such as identify entity, retrieve support, verify bridge fact, and answer, which is especially useful when direct prompting underperforms on knowledge-intensive QA.
predictions: Largest gains appear on 3-4 hop questions.
Answer F1 rises while unsupported intermediate facts drop.
minimal_test: Run GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B-Instruct on HotpotQA distractor and 2WikiMultiHopQA using a transfer prompt adapted from pseudo-code prompting: require outputs in fixed steps {extract entities; propose bridge entity; select supporting sentences; derive answer}. Compare against standard CoT prompting and the published InfoRE-style reorganization prompt as baselines. Evaluate Answer F1/EM on both datasets and supporting-fact F1 on HotpotQA.

scope_conditions.method: pseudo-code prompting with fixed symbolic hop operators
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-hop-QA with explicit evidence paragraphs

evidence_gap: No direct experiment has tested pseudo-code-style reasoning prompts from graph tasks on standard multi-hop-QA benchmarks, nor measured whether gains come from better hop decomposition versus verbosity.

hypothesis: Meta-reasoning prompting from multi-step reasoning could improve multi-hop-QA by first selecting a reasoning strategy for the question type before generating the answer path.
mechanism: A prompt that asks the model to choose among strategies such as comparison, bridge-entity chaining, temporal ordering, or verification may better match heterogeneous multi-hop questions, while avoiding one-size-fits-all prompting that can fail on mixed reasoning tasks.
predictions: Bridge-comparison questions benefit more than single-relation questions.
Stronger models gain more than weaker models.
minimal_test: Implement a Meta-Reasoning Prompting transfer on HotpotQA and StrategyQA with GPT-4o and GPT-3.5-turbo: step 1 classify the question into one of four reasoning strategies; step 2 answer using the selected template; step 3 provide final answer only. Baselines are zero-shot direct prompting and vanilla CoT, plus InfoRE on the same models. Metrics are Answer F1/EM for HotpotQA and accuracy for StrategyQA; stratify results by annotated question type where available.

scope_conditions.method: meta-reasoning prompting with explicit strategy selection
scope_conditions.task: heterogeneous multi-hop-QA requiring mixed reasoning patterns

evidence_gap: It remains untested whether strategy-selection prompts transfer beyond synthetic or general reasoning tasks into open-domain multi-hop-QA, and whether any benefit persists after controlling for extra prompt length.

hypothesis: Graph-based in-context example retrieval from multi-step reasoning could improve multi-hop-QA by selecting demonstrations whose entity-relation structure matches the target question's hop topology.
mechanism: Retrieving demonstrations by structural similarity rather than lexical similarity may supply more useful exemplars for bridge and comparison questions, analogous to gains seen when reasoning examples are organized by graph structure.
predictions: Structural retrieval beats BM25 retrieval for bridge questions.
Benefits shrink when only one in-context example is allowed.
minimal_test: Construct a demonstration pool from HotpotQA training data where each example is converted into a small question-evidence graph over entities and supporting sentences. At inference on HotpotQA dev and WikiHop dev, retrieve 4 demonstrations using graph-structure similarity (shared hop count, bridge vs comparison topology, entity overlap constraints) and place them into a few-shot prompt for GPT-4o-mini. Compare against random few-shot, BM25 lexical retrieval, and automatically generated in-context examples as baselines. Evaluate Answer F1/EM and supporting-fact F1 on HotpotQA.

scope_conditions.method: graph-based in-context example retrieval for few-shot prompting
scope_conditions.task: multi-hop-QA with reusable question-evidence topology
