minimal_test: Implement a 2-agent multimodal pipeline on MMVET and MuCR using GPT-4o or LLaVA-Next as both actor and critic with role prompts: actor produces stepwise rationale and answer from image+question; critic inspects the image and flags unsupported steps; actor revises once. Compare against the same base model in single-pass chain-of-thought and self-consistency baselines. Evaluate with accuracy on MMVET and MuCR (C2E/CP/EXP), plus manual error counts for missed visual cues on a 100-example subset.

scope_conditions.method: critic-actor interaction and multimodal agent prompting
scope_conditions.task: complex visual reasoning and multimodal causal reasoning where image evidence must support multiple reasoning steps

evidence_gap: No direct experiment yet isolates whether agent-style revision helps multimodal reasoning because of better reasoning control versus extra inference budget.

hypothesis: Sparse/grouped multi-agent communication strategies from language-agent debate will transfer to multimodal reasoning by preserving most accuracy while reducing visual-token and context costs on long-horizon image or video tasks.
mechanism: Multimodal reasoning often wastes tokens through redundant full-history sharing; restricting communication to grouped or sparse topologies should keep diverse hypotheses while avoiding repeated re-encoding of visual context.
predictions: Token cost drops at least 25% on TiM versus full debate.
Accuracy remains within 2 points of dense debate on Mementos.
minimal_test: Run multimodal multi-agent debate with 6 agents on TiM and Mementos using a fixed VLM backbone such as Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Compare three communication topologies: dense all-to-all debate, sparse ring, and 3+3 group discussion. Keep the same number of total agent calls and one final judge. Baselines are single-agent CoT and dense debate. Measure F1 on TiM, F1 on Mementos, and total prompt+completion tokens including image/frame references.

scope_conditions.method: sparse communication topology or grouped discussion for multimodal multi-agent systems
scope_conditions.task: video or image-sequence multi-step reasoning with long contexts

evidence_gap: Existing token-efficiency findings are mostly from text-agent settings or isolated multimodal debates, not from controlled transfers to sequence-heavy multimodal benchmarks.

hypothesis: Agent role specialization with modality-specific subagents will help multimodal multi-step reasoning most on tasks with known perception bottlenecks, but gains will saturate or reverse when too many rounds amplify noisy visual interpretations.
mechanism: Separating perception, verifier, and planner roles can decompose failures on spatial/causal benchmarks, yet additional rounds may propagate early perceptual mistakes or overconfidence instead of correcting them.
predictions: Three specialized agents outperform one monolithic VLM on TopViewRS EM.
More than four rounds reduces accuracy on CDR relative-direction questions.
minimal_test: Build a 3-role multimodal agent system for TopViewRS and CDR with a perception agent (extract objects/relations from image), planner agent (derive multistep solution), and verifier agent (check consistency against image). Use Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct or GPT-4o as the shared backbone with role-specific prompts. Compare against the same backbone with single-agent CoT and against an unstructured 3-agent debate. Sweep rounds from 1 to 6. Metrics: EM/PM on TopViewRS and accuracy on CDR relative/absolute direction tasks.

scope_conditions.method: role-specialized multimodal agents with bounded interaction rounds
scope_conditions.task: spatial and causal multimodal reasoning where perception errors are a major bottleneck

evidence_gap: It remains untested whether role specialization transfers cleanly from text-agent collaboration to multimodal settings, especially under controlled round-count sweeps and perception-heavy tasks.

hypothesis: Supervising a single fine-tuned model with agent-style critique-revision traces will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy over standard answer-only or chain-of-thought fine-tuning, especially on hard examples.
mechanism: Agent systems appear to gain from explicit critic-to-actor refinement and problem-specific action descriptions; distilling those intermediate revisions into supervised trajectories may teach the model when to revise erroneous substeps rather than only imitate final answers.
predictions: Critique-trace SFT beats answer-only SFT on LogiQA accuracy.
Gains concentrate on multi-hop subsets more than easy subsets.
minimal_test: Generate training data on GSM8K and LogiQA by running an agent pipeline with one actor and one critic that produces initial solution, critique, and revised solution for each training item; fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct with (a) final-answer-only SFT baseline, (b) standard CoT SFT baseline, and (c) critique-revision SFT transfer condition; evaluate exact-match/accuracy on GSM8K and LogiQA, plus step-level edit acceptance rate on a held-out set of generated critiques.

scope_conditions.method: agent-style critic-actor trace distillation into supervised fine-tuning
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-step reasoning with available training labels and rationale generation budget

evidence_gap: No direct evidence here tests whether the critic-actor interaction benefit survives compression into a single fine-tuned model rather than requiring online multi-agent inference.

hypothesis: Agent-derived diversity can transfer to fine-tuning if synthetic training data is constructed from disagreements among multiple solvers, with positive and negative trajectories both retained, yielding better robustness than fine-tuning on only consensus or only correct chains.
mechanism: Several agent results suggest benefits come from diversity and peer review, while fine-tuning work hints that negative samples and explanation supervision matter; disagreement-conditioned data may expose boundary cases and prevent overconfident collapse to one reasoning style.
predictions: Disagreement-aware SFT lowers calibration error versus consensus-only SFT.
Benefit is larger on out-of-distribution graph or spatial splits.
minimal_test: On StepGame and CLUTRR, sample 4 independent agent solutions per training example using heterogeneous prompting or models, label agreement patterns, and build three fine-tuning corpora for Mistral-7B-Instruct: consensus-only correct traces, mixed correct+incorrect disagreement traces with correctness tags, and standard synthetic graph-data SFT baseline; train with identical token budgets and evaluate accuracy on in-domain and longer-hop test sets, plus expected calibration error and Brier score against the consensus-only baseline.

scope_conditions.method: multi-agent disagreement mining for synthetic supervision with correctness tags
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks where multiple sampled solution paths can be cheaply generated

evidence_gap: The payload contains separate evidence for agent diversity and for synthetic/negative-data fine-tuning, but not for combining disagreement structure with fine-tuning objectives or calibration-focused evaluation.

hypothesis: Communication-topology ideas from multi-agent reasoning can be transferred into parameter-efficient fine-tuning by training structured modular adapters with asymmetric centrality, producing similar reasoning gains at lower trainable-parameter cost than uniform LoRA.
mechanism: Agent studies report that sparse/grouped communication and central placement of stronger components can improve cost-performance tradeoffs; an analogous fine-tuning design would assign larger or cross-layer adapters to central reasoning layers and smaller adapters elsewhere, encouraging staged information aggregation inside one model.
predictions: Centrality-weighted adapters outperform uniform LoRA at equal trainable-parameter budget.
Sparse grouped adapters reduce training FLOPs with no more than 1 point accuracy loss.
minimal_test: Implement a centrality-weighted LoRA scheme on LLaVA-7B or InstructBLIP for MathVerse or ScanQA: allocate higher ranks to middle/high-impact transformer blocks and low ranks to peripheral blocks, and compare against uniform-rank LoRA and full fine-tuning baselines under the same total trainable-parameter budget; report accuracy/EM, trainable-parameter count, and training FLOPs, with an ablation for sparse grouped adapter sharing across block groups.

scope_conditions.method: parameter-efficient fine-tuning with topology-inspired nonuniform adapter allocation
scope_conditions.task: multimodal or text multi-step reasoning where PEFT is already feasible

evidence_gap: The analogy between external agent communication topology and internal adapter topology has not been directly tested, so it is unknown whether agent centrality effects map onto layerwise fine-tuning structure.

hypothesis: Actor-critic style agent interaction transferred into tool-use pipelines will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy by selectively revising intermediate tool calls rather than accepting first-pass tool outputs.
mechanism: A critic module can inspect each proposed tool invocation and its returned evidence, then request targeted refinements to arguments, tool choice, or decomposition, reducing error propagation across steps.
predictions: One critique round raises EM over the same tool pipeline without critique.
More than four critique rounds stops helping or slightly hurts token-efficient performance.
minimal_test: Implement an actor-critic wrapper around MACT for complex table question answering on CRT: the actor generates the next tool call and rationale, the critic reviews the call/output and may request one revision before execution. Compare against vanilla MACT and self-consistency SC(Qw+CL). Report Exact Match and token cost per question; add an ablation with 1, 2, and 5 critique rounds.

scope_conditions.method: critic-actor interaction transferred from agent reasoning to tool-use execution
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning with external tools, especially table QA or visual reasoning pipelines with editable intermediate tool calls

evidence_gap: No direct experiment shows that critique dynamics that help agent reasoning also improve tool-call sequencing rather than only adding overhead.

hypothesis: Agent grouping and sparse communication strategies will transfer to tool-use reasoning by organizing tools into small coordinated subteams, improving cost-accuracy tradeoffs over flat tool selection.
mechanism: Partitioning tools into groups or hierarchical neighborhoods can limit cross-step context bloat while preserving diversity of intermediate evidence, analogous to multi-agent group discussion and sparse debate topologies.
predictions: Grouped tool routing cuts token cost versus flat all-tools prompting.
A 3+3 grouped tool topology outperforms ungrouped routing on accuracy-cost Pareto efficiency.
minimal_test: On SEED with LLaVA+P2G, replace flat access to all grounding/auxiliary tools with grouped routing: first choose one of two 3-tool groups, then allow only intra-group tool exchanges before final answer generation. Baselines are standard LLaVA+P2G with flat tool access and a hierarchical tool baseline with no grouping heuristic. Report answer accuracy, average prompt+response tokens, and Pareto dominance across simple and hard SEED splits.

scope_conditions.method: group discussion and sparse communication topology adapted to tool routing
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning where multiple tools are available and not all need to be consulted each step

evidence_gap: Existing tool-use papers argue for hierarchy or modularity, but not explicit group-discussion-style topologies imported from agent coordination policies.

hypothesis: Profile- and role-conditioned decomposition from multi-agent reasoning will transfer to tool-use by assigning semantically specialized tool roles and step descriptions, yielding better intermediate question formulation than generic tool invocation.
mechanism: When each tool is invoked with an explicit role profile and problem-specific action description, the model can generate more discriminative subquestions and choose better arguments, especially on heterogeneous multi-step tasks.
predictions: Role-labeled tool prompts outperform identical tools with generic prompts.
Removing step-specific action descriptions causes a measurable accuracy drop.
minimal_test: Extend LATM on Logical Deduction (5) and Tracking Shuffled Objects (5) so each generated tool is paired with a role card (e.g., state tracker, constraint checker, arithmetic verifier) plus a problem-specific action description for the current substep. Compare against vanilla LATM and a role-only ablation without action descriptions. Report accuracy and tool-selection precision measured as the fraction of steps where the chosen tool matches a human-written oracle tool category on a 200-example annotated subset.

scope_conditions.method: agent profiles and action descriptions transferred to tool prompting and decomposition
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning tasks with reusable tools whose utility depends on subproblem semantics

evidence_gap: Tool-use work shows decomposition and tool reuse, but lacks controlled tests of whether agent-style role profiles and action descriptions causally improve tool selection and subquestion quality.

hypothesis: Introducing an agent-style critic-actor refinement loop inside search-based reasoning will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy by pruning false-positive branches more reliably than search alone.
mechanism: A separate critic can provide branch-local feedback before expansion, turning actor revisions into a lightweight learned heuristic that complements reward-guided search and reduces commitment to superficially plausible chains.
predictions: Higher step-level accuracy than plain search
Fewer explored false-positive branches at equal budget
minimal_test: Implement a critic-augmented version of reward-guided search on GSM8K: at each expansion, generate candidate next steps with the base LLM, score each with a separate critic prompt, revise once via actor conditioned on critic feedback, then continue search. Compare against the original reward-guided search baseline and direct chain-of-thought decoding using the same backbone model. Evaluate final answer accuracy, step-level accuracy on annotated traces if available, and average tokens per solved problem.

scope_conditions.method: agent critic-actor refinement transferred into reward-guided search or TSE-style expansion
scope_conditions.task: text multi-step reasoning where intermediate steps can be scored or revised

evidence_gap: No direct evidence yet shows that agent-style critique improves branch selection within search-based inference rather than only in standalone multi-agent interaction.

hypothesis: Transferring sparse/grouped multi-agent communication patterns to search-based inference will preserve most reasoning gains while reducing the token cost of broad search.
mechanism: Search trees often pay for redundant sibling exploration; grouping candidate branches and allowing only periodic cross-branch information exchange can approximate breadth advantages while avoiding full pairwise comparison among all candidates.
predictions: Token usage drops versus unconstrained breadth search
Accuracy stays within 1-2 points of full search at fixed model
minimal_test: Build a grouped AR-MCTS variant on StrategyQA or HotpotQA where frontier nodes are partitioned into 3-branch groups, each group shares summaries internally, and only one representative summary per group is propagated globally every expansion round. Compare against standard AR-MCTS or breadth-heavy reward-guided search with the same rollout budget and backbone model. Report EM/accuracy, total generated tokens, and solved-problems-per-dollar.

scope_conditions.method: grouped or sparse communication over search frontier nodes
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks where breadth is important and many sibling branches are explored

evidence_gap: Existing evidence supports token savings from sparse agent communication and accuracy benefits from breadth in search, but not their joint use in a single search controller.

hypothesis: Applying agent-style role specialization and capability-aware assignment to search-based reasoning will help smaller models benefit more from search by allocating distinct planner, verifier, and executor functions across search stages.
mechanism: Role specialization can reduce error propagation by matching subproblems to prompts or models best suited for planning, checking, or execution; this may be especially helpful when search already amplifies weak local decisions and when smaller backbones gain disproportionately from structured guidance.
predictions: Smaller models gain more from role-specialized search than larger models
Verifier-assigned search beats homogeneous search under same expansion budget
minimal_test: Create a role-specialized AR-MCTS on MATH and BBH using one backbone model with three prompts: planner proposes actions, executor expands steps, verifier scores consistency before backup; optionally place the strongest available model only in the verifier role in a mixed-model setting. Compare to homogeneous AR-MCTS using the same total calls and to a simple self-consistency baseline. Measure answer accuracy, verifier rejection rate of bad branches, and total token/call budget.

scope_conditions.method: role-specialized search with planner/verifier/executor prompts or mixed-model node assignment
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with decomposable intermediate states and constrained inference budget

evidence_gap: There is no direct test showing that agent-inspired role assignment, or central placement of a stronger component, transfers to search node expansion and backup policies.

hypothesis: Injecting an explicit agent-style critic-actor split into self-refine decoding will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy over intrinsic self-correction by making revisions more likely to target identified errors rather than rephrase the original answer.
mechanism: Agent papers suggest structured critique is actually acted on and task-specific guidance matters; transferring that to self-refine could reduce answer-retention failure by separating error localization from answer rewriting.
predictions: Higher answer-change rate after critique
Accuracy gain over vanilla self-correct on GSM8K
minimal_test: Run GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 on GSM8K and CommonSenseQA with three conditions: standard prompting, vanilla intrinsic self-correct, and transferred critic-actor self-refine where one prompt generates a labeled critique and a second prompt must revise only the criticized spans. Baseline is vanilla intrinsic self-correct from arxiv:2310.01798v2#c01; metrics are exact-match/accuracy and answer-change rate between draft and final.

scope_conditions.method: agent-inspired critic-actor prompting transferred into self-refine inference
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-step reasoning where intermediate rationale can be externally critiqued

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests whether role-separated critique and revision, without adding multiple independent agents, fixes intrinsic self-correction failures on standard reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Transferring agent communication sparsification and early-stop policies to self-refine will preserve or improve reasoning accuracy while reducing the token cost of iterative refinement.
mechanism: Agent results indicate too many rounds can hurt and grouped/sparse communication lowers cost; in self-refine, restricting refinement to a small number of targeted edits or stopping after critique confidence saturates may prevent degradation from over-editing.
predictions: Fewer refinement turns reduce token usage by >20%
Accuracy peaks within 1-2 refine turns
minimal_test: Evaluate MiniCPM-Llama3-V2.5 on RealWorldQA and SEEDBench with four inference settings: initial generation, vanilla 3-turn intrinsic self-correction, sparse self-refine with only one critique sentence plus one revised answer per turn, and adaptive early-stop self-refine that halts when two consecutive critiques identify no new error category. Baseline is vanilla multi-turn intrinsic self-correction from arxiv:2410.04055v3#c03 and #c04; metrics are accuracy and total output tokens per question.

scope_conditions.method: round-limited or sparsified self-refine protocol inspired by agent debate scheduling
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks where repeated intrinsic correction currently causes drift or verbosity

evidence_gap: The payload contains no head-to-head experiment applying debate-style sparsity or round scheduling to self-refine loops, especially on benchmarks showing multi-turn degradation.

hypothesis: Training self-refine models on diversified role-conditioned revision trajectories derived from agent collaboration patterns will outperform standard self-refine instruction-tuning on harder multi-step reasoning tasks by increasing solution diversity without requiring multi-agent inference at test time.
mechanism: Agent collaboration gains appear to come partly from diverse viewpoints and peer review, while self-refine training gains come from iterative improvement; combining them in training could teach one model to simulate multiple complementary reviewers internally.
predictions: Self-refine-tuned model shows larger gains on SVAMP than GSM8K
Single-model test-time inference matches or beats multi-sample self-refine baseline
minimal_test: Create a training set from GSM8K and SVAMP where each item contains an initial answer plus three synthetic role-conditioned critiques modeled on agent peer review (e.g., arithmetic checker, assumption checker, alternative-solution reviewer) and a final revised answer. Fine-tune Llama-2-7B with this agent-pattern self-refine instruction-tuning and compare against the standard self-refine instruction-tuning baseline from arxiv:2405.00402v1#c01 on GSM8K and SVAMP. Metrics are accuracy and average tokens at test time under single-pass generation plus one optional revision.

scope_conditions.method: agent-patterned self-refine instruction-tuning
scope_conditions.task: small/open-weight models on math and symbolic multi-step reasoning with enough training data for supervised refinement traces

evidence_gap: Existing claims support agent diversity and self-refine tuning separately, but there is no direct evidence that agent-style role diversity can be distilled into a single self-refining model for reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Fine-tuning multimodal reasoning models with explicit raw-visual-cue supervision and intermediate rationales could reduce the recurrent failure mode where models rely on abstract textual shortcuts instead of grounded multi-step reasoning.
mechanism: Claims about Form-3 and guided vision suggest that preserving direct visual evidence improves cue extraction, while fine-tuning claims suggest rationale-supervised adaptation can teach the model to use those cues during answer generation.
predictions: Rationale-supervised fine-tuning will raise MuCR accuracy above vanilla SFT.
Cue-grounded rationales will reduce errors on behavior-heavy Mementos subsets.
minimal_test: Take LLaVA-7B as the base model and fine-tune it on a mixed training set built from MuCR and Mementos using chain-of-thought annotations that explicitly reference visual entities/cues in the input, then compare against (1) the same model with answer-only supervised fine-tuning and (2) the untuned base LLaVA-7B. Evaluate on MuCR with accuracy and on Mementos with F1, plus rationale grounding rate measured by whether mentioned entities/actions are visually present.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with cue-grounded chain-of-thought supervision transferred from multimodal raw-visual reasoning setups
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step reasoning where failures stem from missed visual cues rather than missing world knowledge

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests whether visual-cue-preserving input formats combined with rationale-focused fine-tuning outperform answer-only tuning on the same multimodal reasoning benchmark.

hypothesis: Injecting structured spatial signals from multimodal models, such as depth or coarse correspondences, into fine-tuning data and adapters could disproportionately improve fine-tuned performance on spatial multi-step reasoning benchmarks that remain weak under generic supervision.
mechanism: Multimodal claims indicate spatial reasoning improves when models receive geometry-aligned signals like depth or correspondences; transferring these signals into the fine-tuning stage may make supervision more factorized and easier to learn than generic visual-text instruction tuning.
predictions: Depth-augmented fine-tuning will improve BLINK Relative Depth accuracy over standard LoRA.
Correspondence-augmented fine-tuning will improve ScanQA accuracy over answer-only tuning.
minimal_test: Start from InstructBLIP and run two LoRA fine-tuning variants on BLINK Relative Depth and ScanQA: (1) standard image-question-answer SFT and (2) spatial-signal SFT where each example additionally includes monocular depth maps for BLINK or coarse correspondence tokens for ScanQA. Use the same train split and trainable-parameter budget. Baselines are vanilla InstructBLIP and standard LoRA SFT. Report accuracy on BLINK Relative Depth and exact-match/accuracy on ScanQA.

scope_conditions.method: parameter-efficient fine-tuning augmented with geometry-aware multimodal signals
scope_conditions.task: spatial multi-step reasoning tasks where ambiguity can be resolved by depth, correspondences, or explicit scene geometry

evidence_gap: The payload contains evidence that spatial signals help multimodal inference and that fine-tuning helps reasoning, but not a direct transfer experiment where those spatial signals are encoded as part of the fine-tuning procedure under matched budgets.

hypothesis: Multimodal sequential-input advantages can be converted into more robust fine-tuning curricula by training on temporally ordered visual reasoning examples before static reasoning tasks, yielding better compositional generalization than single-task fine-tuning alone.
mechanism: Sequential multimodal evidence suggests ordered observations help reasoning over latent state changes; a curriculum that first fine-tunes on image/video sequences may teach reusable transition reasoning that transfers to static but multi-hop tasks such as graph or spatial reasoning.
predictions: Sequence-first curriculum will outperform direct fine-tuning on TiM F1.
Sequence-first curriculum will improve out-of-domain graph reasoning accuracy.
minimal_test: Use LLaVA-7B and compare three training regimes: (1) direct fine-tuning on GraphSolver graph reasoning data only, (2) direct fine-tuning on TiM video reasoning data only, and (3) a curriculum that first fine-tunes on TiM with dense frame sampling and then fine-tunes on GraphSolver. Evaluate on TiM with F1 and on GraphSolver out-of-domain tasks with accuracy, using the direct GraphSolver fine-tune as the primary baseline.

scope_conditions.method: curriculum fine-tuning transferred from multimodal sequence reasoning to downstream multi-step reasoning
scope_conditions.task: tasks requiring latent state transition tracking, compositional dependency chaining, or long-horizon inference

evidence_gap: There is no direct evidence in the payload that sequence-oriented multimodal fine-tuning transfers to non-sequence reasoning benchmarks, especially under out-of-domain generalization settings.

hypothesis: Sequential multimodal state-tracking methods could improve tool-use multi-step reasoning by making intermediate tool outputs explicit state objects that the planner reasons over rather than only textual summaries.
mechanism: Multimodal work suggests direct access to evolving raw inputs and sequence structure improves multi-step reasoning; transferring that idea to tool-use may reduce state-loss between steps when tools return images, tables, or other artifacts.
predictions: State-tracking improves exact-answer accuracy on visual tool-use tasks.
Gains are larger on longer tool chains than on 1-step tasks.
minimal_test: Implement a tool-use agent on SEED using LLaVA 7B + P2G as baseline from arxiv:2403.19322v2#c01, then add a sequential state memory module that stores each intermediate tool output as an image/text state and prompts the planner over the full ordered state history; compare against vanilla LLaVA+P2G on SEED hard questions using Accuracy and on P2GB using object/text accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: sequential state memory over multimodal tool outputs
scope_conditions.task: multi-step visual reasoning with external tools that emit intermediate artifacts

evidence_gap: No direct experiment shows that sequence-aware multimodal state representations transfer to general tool-use planners rather than pure image-sequence understanding.

hypothesis: Perception-guidance techniques from multimodal reasoning could make tool selection and invocation more reliable in tool-use reasoning by surfacing task-relevant evidence before the planner commits to a tool.
mechanism: Claims about guided vision, raw visual access, and grounding suggest early disambiguation of salient cues can shift failures from perception to reasoning; in tool-use settings this may prevent wrong tool calls caused by misread inputs.
predictions: Guided evidence extraction reduces wrong-tool-call rate.
Benefits are strongest on nuanced object and high-resolution questions.
minimal_test: Take LLaVA 7B + P2G on P2GB and SEED as the baseline from arxiv:2403.19322v2#c01 and arxiv:2403.19322v2#c02; add a pre-tool perception-guidance stage that first asks the model to output grounded regions/attributes relevant to the question before selecting a tool, then executes the same tool set; evaluate against baseline using answer Accuracy on SEED, object/text accuracy on P2GB, and a logged tool-selection error rate.

scope_conditions.method: guided perception-to-tool routing with explicit grounded evidence
scope_conditions.task: tool-use reasoning where tool choice depends on fine-grained visual cues

evidence_gap: Existing evidence shows guidance helps multimodal reasoning and grounding helps tool-use, but not that guidance specifically improves downstream tool routing decisions.

hypothesis: Rationale-first multimodal reasoning transfers to tool-use by generating structured subgoal rationales before tool execution, which may improve decomposition quality and tool hierarchy use.
mechanism: Multimodal CoT and explainer-style methods indicate better intermediate rationales correlate with answer quality; combining them with hierarchical tool-use may help the agent choose smaller, more compositional subproblems and offload only the right operations.
predictions: Structured rationale-first planning improves final accuracy over direct tool calling.
Rationale quality correlates with fewer redundant tool invocations.
minimal_test: Use the least-to-most visual reasoning with external tools framework from arxiv:2406.19934v2#c02 as baseline on a visual reasoning benchmark such as SEED; add a rationale-first planner that produces a JSON subgoal chain with evidence slots and tool candidates before any tool call, then executes the same tools; compare against the original planner using Accuracy on SEED and average number of tool calls per solved example as an efficiency metric.

scope_conditions.method: structured rationale-first planning before hierarchical tool execution
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks where tools can be arranged into decomposable subgoals

evidence_gap: There is no direct transfer evidence that rationale gains observed in multimodal answer generation persist when rationales are used to control external tool programs.

graph_bridge.to: creating tools with a clear hierarchy

hypothesis: Applying reward-guided search over multimodal rationale candidates could improve hard visual reasoning accuracy by pruning perceptually plausible but logically inconsistent chains.
mechanism: Search-based scoring can treat each intermediate visual-text rationale as a state and use answer consistency plus step-level verifier rewards to suppress false-positive chains, matching claims that multimodal models often fail after perception while search reduces false positives.
predictions: Largest gains occur on TopViewRS Dynamic Spatial Reasoning over direct CoT.
Verifier-guided breadth-4 search beats self-consistency at equal token budget.
minimal_test: Implement reward-guided beam search on top of GPT-4o or LLaVA-1.5 for TopViewRS, where each step proposes a visual-text subclaim and a verifier scores consistency with the image and question; compare against direct decoding and self-consistency baselines using Exact Match and Partial Match on TopViewRS.

scope_conditions.method: reward-guided search transferred from search-based step-by-step reasoning to multimodal chain-of-thought generation
scope_conditions.task: top-view and spatial multimodal multi-step reasoning with explicit intermediate rationales

evidence_gap: No direct experiment yet isolates whether search helps after visual grounding errors versus only after textual reasoning errors in multimodal benchmarks.

hypothesis: Breadth-first thought expansion from search-based reasoning will help multimodal sequence reasoning more than deeper single-chain rollouts because image/video tasks contain multiple plausible event hypotheses that benefit from parallel exploration.
mechanism: When evidence is temporally ambiguous, broader exploration can preserve competing interpretations of object state and behavior before committing, analogous to claims that breadth matters more than depth in reasoning-space search and that multimodal sequence models struggle especially on behavior reasoning.
predictions: Breadth-8 shallow search improves behavior F1 on Mementos more than depth-8 rollouts.
Benefit is larger for behavior questions than object questions on Mementos.
minimal_test: Take GPT-4V or Gemini as the base model on Mementos and TiM, implement two search policies over intermediate event hypotheses: breadth-first expansion with width 8 and depth 2 versus depth-oriented rollout with width 2 and depth 8; compare to direct sequential prompting baseline using F1 on Mementos and TiM, with separate reporting for object versus behavior subsets on Mementos.

scope_conditions.method: breadth-prioritized search policy transferred to multimodal temporal reasoning
scope_conditions.task: image-sequence and video multi-step reasoning with latent event-state ambiguity

evidence_gap: Existing multimodal results compare input formats and frame rates, but do not test whether search-width versus search-depth is the main driver under fixed compute.

hypothesis: Trajectory-generated self-improvement from search-based reasoning could produce better multimodal reasoning finetuning data than reranked direct outputs, especially for smaller vision-language models.
mechanism: Search can synthesize diverse successful trajectories that expose alternative visual grounding and reasoning paths; training on these trajectories may improve intermediate-step robustness, with stronger relative gains in smaller MLLMs where search already appears more helpful.
predictions: Qwen2-VL-7B finetuned on search-generated trajectories outperforms reranked-trajectory finetuning on MBARD accuracy.
Relative gain is larger for 7B models than for GPT-4o prompting-only adaptation.
minimal_test: Use AR-MCTS or TSE to generate successful multimodal reasoning trajectories for Qwen2-VL-7B on MBARD or SMART, finetune one model on search-generated trajectories and another on equal-sized reranked direct-decoding trajectories, then evaluate against the original backbone and reranked-trajectory baseline using Accuracy on MBARD or SMART.

scope_conditions.method: search-generated trajectory self-improvement transferred to multimodal finetuning
scope_conditions.task: multimodal analogical or algorithmic multi-step reasoning in small-to-mid-size VLMs

evidence_gap: There is no direct evidence that search-generated trajectories remain beneficial once visual grounding noise is included in the training targets.

hypothesis: Applying externally grounded self-refine to multimodal multi-step reasoning will improve visual reasoning accuracy when the refinement stage is conditioned on explicit visual evidence rather than only the model's prior answer.
mechanism: Multimodal failures often stem from missed visual cues or weak perception grounding, so a self-refine loop that must re-attend to image regions/frames and critique whether each reasoning step is visually supported could avoid the degradation seen in intrinsic self-correction while capturing the benefits of feedback-guided refinement.
predictions: Visual-grounded critique beats vanilla self-correction on RealWorldQA.
Gains are larger on cue-sensitive tasks than on text-dominant ones.
minimal_test: Run MiniCPM-Llama3-V2.5 or Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct on RealWorldQA and CLEVR with three settings: direct answer, intrinsic self-correction baseline using the VP-1 style re-answer prompt, and a new visual-grounded self-refine prompt that requires citing image evidence for each correction. Measure Accuracy, and additionally track answer-change precision (fraction of changed answers that become correct).

scope_conditions.method: self-refine with explicit visual-evidence critique
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step reasoning where the answer depends on localized or relational visual cues

evidence_gap: No direct study has isolated whether externally grounded visual critique, rather than intrinsic rephrasing, is the ingredient needed to make self-refine help multimodal reasoning.

hypothesis: Using multimodal intermediate representations as the object of refinement, rather than refining only final natural-language answers, will make self-refine more effective on spatial and temporal multi-step reasoning.
mechanism: Results on multimodal reasoning suggest that enriched intermediate structures such as depth, sequence ordering, scene metadata, or rationale traces improve reasoning; self-refine may work better if it edits these latent structured representations first and only then regenerates the answer, reducing error propagation from an initially flawed verbal explanation.
predictions: Structure-first refinement improves TopViewRS EM over answer-only refinement.
Depth-augmented refinement helps relative-depth questions more than generic VQA.
minimal_test: On TopViewRS and BLINK Relative Depth, compare four variants of a single open MLLM such as Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct: zero-shot direct answer, answer-only self-refine, structure-then-answer self-refine where the model first outputs and revises a scene graph/depth relation table, and structure-then-answer with provided scene metadata. Baselines are direct answer and answer-only self-refine; metrics are EM and PM for TopViewRS and Accuracy for BLINK Relative Depth.

scope_conditions.method: self-refine over multimodal structured intermediates
scope_conditions.task: spatial or temporal reasoning tasks with recoverable latent structure such as depth, trajectories, or object relations

evidence_gap: Existing self-refine work mostly evaluates textual answer revision, while multimodal work shows benefit from richer representations but does not test iterative refinement over those representations.

hypothesis: Curriculum-style self-training from the self-refine cluster can transfer to multimodal reasoning by generating progressively harder visual reasoning traces, yielding larger gains than one-shot distillation on benchmarks where current MLLMs are near random or far below humans.
mechanism: When multimodal reasoning is bottlenecked by scarce high-quality reasoning supervision, iterative self-training with filtering and replay may bootstrap better multimodal chains of thought; the effect should be strongest on hard compositional tasks where simple prompting and intrinsic correction are unstable but synthetic trace accumulation can improve coverage.
predictions: Iterative self-training beats GPT-distilled one-pass fine-tuning on TiM F1.
Benefits concentrate on long-range compositional and causal subsets.
minimal_test: Implement an R3V-style pipeline for Qwen-VL or LLaVA-Next on TiM and MuCR: seed the model with direct-answer and CoT generations, filter for consistency with the gold label or a verifier, fine-tune, regenerate on harder examples, and repeat for 2-3 rounds. Compare against supervised fine-tuning on the same data and a one-shot GPT-distilled rationale baseline. Report TiM F1 and MuCR Accuracy, plus breakdowns by abstract perception/long-range compositional categories.

scope_conditions.method: iterative self-training with refined multimodal rationales
scope_conditions.task: hard multimodal multi-step reasoning with enough training data or synthetic generation budget to support multiple refinement rounds

evidence_gap: Multimodal self-training gains have been shown in some vision-language reasoning settings, but not on the hardest multi-step causal, temporal, and compositional benchmarks highlighted here, and not in direct comparison to one-shot distillation under matched budgets.

hypothesis: Intermediate-step fine-tuning from graph/spatial reasoning could make tool-using agents plan more faithful multi-step tool sequences, improving tool-use accuracy on compositional reasoning benchmarks.
mechanism: Supervision on explicit intermediate reasoning states may teach a latent planner that decomposes a problem into ordered subgoals before selecting tools, reducing tool misselection and premature answer emission.
predictions: Tool-call accuracy rises over zero-shot tool use
Benefit is largest on longer-hop reasoning items
minimal_test: Take a LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct tool-use agent and supervised-fine-tune it on GraphSolver+-style intermediate step traces derived from StepGame or DFS-style graph tasks, then evaluate the same model with access to LATM-style or Questioner-style tools on BBH logical deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects. Baselines: identical tool-use agent without the intermediate-step SFT, and CoT prompting with the same tools. Metrics: task accuracy and exact-match tool-call sequence accuracy.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with intermediate reasoning-step supervision transferred into a tool-using planner
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks where solutions can be decomposed into 3+ ordered subproblems with available external tools

evidence_gap: No direct experiment shows that intermediate-step supervised traces learned in pure fine-tuning transfer to downstream tool-selection behavior rather than only to answer generation.

hypothesis: Synthetic fine-tuning data that encode executable structures such as graphs or code could improve tool-use more than generic instruction tuning by teaching models to emit tool arguments and subproblem structure more systematically.
mechanism: Structured synthetic data may induce stronger representations of variables, dependencies, and state transitions, which map naturally onto API arguments and chained tool invocation.
predictions: Structured-data SFT beats generic SFT before tool execution
25% structured data outperforms 50% on some tasks
minimal_test: Fine-tune Mistral-7B-Instruct in three conditions before adding the same calculator and Python tools: (1) generic instruction tuning, (2) synthetic graph-reasoning SFT using StepGame-style generated traces, and (3) code-heavy SFT matching the token budget of condition 2. Then evaluate all three as tool-using agents on GSM8K and BBH logical deduction with identical tool APIs. Baselines: no extra SFT plus tools, and generic-SFT plus tools. Metrics: final answer accuracy, tool-argument exact match, and average number of tool errors per example.

scope_conditions.method: preparatory fine-tuning on synthetic graph/code data before downstream tool-use inference
scope_conditions.task: symbolic or arithmetic multi-step reasoning where external tools require structured arguments

evidence_gap: Existing claims support structured synthetic SFT for reasoning and tool use separately, but there is no head-to-head transfer study showing that graph/code fine-tuning specifically improves later tool invocation quality.

hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of only the planner/interface components in a tool-using system may match or exceed full adaptation for multi-step reasoning, because the main bottleneck is coordinating tool calls rather than changing core world knowledge.
mechanism: LoRA or PEFT concentrated on planner layers, routing tokens, or tool-interface modules could selectively improve action selection and state tracking while preserving the base model's reasoning priors and reducing overfitting.
predictions: Planner-only LoRA matches full FT on in-domain tasks
Full FT degrades more on unseen tool compositions
minimal_test: Implement a tool-using LLaVA-7B or LLaMA-3.1-8B agent with a planner head that emits tool calls for SEED or P2GB-style visual reasoning plus a held-out unseen composition split. Compare (a) frozen base model with planner-only LoRA, (b) LoRA on all language layers, (c) full fine-tuning, and (d) no fine-tuning. Baselines: the no-fine-tuning tool agent and full fine-tuning. Metrics: benchmark accuracy, unseen-composition accuracy, and tool-call F1.

scope_conditions.method: PEFT/LoRA targeted to tool-planning or interface modules rather than full-model adaptation
scope_conditions.task: multi-step tool-use systems with explicit action tokens or planner modules, especially where data are limited

evidence_gap: PEFT benefits are documented for reasoning fine-tuning, but not for isolating the tool-planning submodule in agentic multi-step tool-use settings with OOD tool composition evaluation.

hypothesis: Supervising factual-QA fine-tuning with explicit intermediate reasoning traces, analogous to multi-step reasoning step supervision, could improve answer exactness and evidence use beyond answer-only QA fine-tuning.
mechanism: Intermediate-step supervision may teach the generator to decompose retrieval evidence into verifiable subclaims before producing the final answer, reducing shortcut memorization and improving use of retrieved context.
predictions: EM rises over answer-only FT on multi-hop QA
Evidence-support rate improves on retrieved-context questions
minimal_test: Fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MuSiQue and HotpotQA with retrieved passages using two conditions: answer-only SFT vs step-supervised SFT where training targets include sentence-level decomposition/rationale plus final answer; compare against direct fine-tuning baseline and implicit RAG fine-tuning baseline; evaluate Exact Match and supporting-facts F1 on HotpotQA and Exact Match on MuSiQue.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with intermediate reasoning step supervision
scope_conditions.task: factual-QA with retrieved multi-hop evidence

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the provided graph tests transferring step-supervised reasoning fine-tuning to factual-QA generation under the same base model and retrieval setup.

hypothesis: Synthetic structured training data used for multi-step reasoning could transfer to factual-QA by creating graph-structured evidence-composition examples, improving robustness on compositional and top-1-retrieval QA.
mechanism: Graph-based synthetic examples may teach the model invariant composition operators over entities and relations, making it better at combining sparse retrieved facts when only one or few passages are available.
predictions: Largest gains appear at top-1 retrieval
Benefits concentrate on compositional QA subsets
minimal_test: Construct synthetic graph-to-text QA pairs from Wikidata triples that require 2-4 hop composition, then fine-tune Mistral-Nemo-12B-Chat for RAG QA with this synthetic data mixed into HotpotQA training; compare against identical fine-tuning without synthetic data and against data-augmented RAG fine-tuning baseline from standard QA augmentation only; evaluate EM and F1 on HotpotQA and MuSiQue under top-1 and top-5 retrieval.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with synthetic graph-based reasoning data
scope_conditions.task: factual-QA requiring compositional evidence aggregation

evidence_gap: The current evidence shows synthetic data helps reasoning and RAG fine-tuning helps QA, but there is no cited test of graph-synthetic reasoning data injected into factual-QA fine-tuning.

hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that help reasoning with limited trainable parameters could transfer to factual-QA, but gains will depend on adapting both retrieval-facing and generation-facing modules rather than only the generator.
mechanism: In factual-QA, answer quality depends on both representation of evidence and generation from evidence; PEFT on only one side may bottleneck transfer, while dual-side adaptation should better align retrieval embeddings and answer formation.
predictions: Dual-module LoRA beats generator-only LoRA in EM
Retriever recall improves only when retriever-side modules are tuned
minimal_test: Build a RAG system with RepLLaMA as dense retriever and Llama-3-8B-Instruct as generator on TriviaQA; compare four training settings: no fine-tuning, generator-only LoRA, retriever-only LoRA, and dual LoRA on both retriever and generator using the same QA supervision; baseline is generator-only LoRA; report Recall@20 for retrieval and Exact Match on TriviaQA.

scope_conditions.method: parameter-efficient fine-tuning across retriever and generator
scope_conditions.task: factual-QA in a RAG pipeline

evidence_gap: The graph contains PEFT gains for reasoning models and separate retriever fine-tuning gains for QA, but lacks a direct transfer study testing whether reasoning-style PEFT strategies help factual-QA when split across pipeline modules.

hypothesis: Intermediate-step supervision from multi-step-reasoning fine-tuning could improve domain-QA when answers require latent decomposition, but only if the intermediate representation is domain-grounded rather than generic chain-of-thought.
mechanism: Reasoning-tuned models appear to benefit from explicit intermediate states and explanations; transferring that recipe to domain-QA may help the model learn question decomposition and evidence alignment, reducing shortcut answering on multi-hop domain questions.
predictions: Step-supervised SFT beats answer-only SFT on multi-hop domain-QA.
Gains shrink on single-fact QA subsets.
minimal_test: Take Llama-3-8B-Instruct and fine-tune it on HotpotQA or 2WikiMultihopQA in two conditions: (1) answer-only supervised fine-tuning baseline, (2) step-supervised fine-tuning where each training target includes decomposed subquestions, cited supporting facts, and final answer. Evaluate against the answer-only baseline and a no-fine-tuning baseline using Exact Match and F1 on the standard dev set; additionally report supporting-fact F1 to test whether intermediate supervision improves evidence grounding.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with explicit intermediate reasoning-step supervision
scope_conditions.task: domain-QA with multi-hop or evidence-composition requirements

evidence_gap: No direct transfer test shows that the intermediate-step supervision gains observed on multi-step-reasoning tasks carry over to domain-QA rather than merely increasing verbosity.

hypothesis: Synthetic structure-preserving data used in reasoning fine-tuning could transfer to domain-QA by teaching latent relation composition, especially for graph- or ontology-backed QA, but may fail when retrieval noise dominates.
mechanism: Synthetic graph and chain-of-thought training may improve the model's ability to compose relations and infer hidden paths; in domain-QA this should help tasks like KBQA or biomedical relation QA where answers depend on traversing structured evidence rather than memorizing facts.
predictions: Synthetic relation-path tuning improves WebQSP Hit@1 over standard SFT.
Benefits are larger on compositional questions than simple lookup questions.
minimal_test: Use Llama-2-7B or Llama-3-8B as a base model on WebQSP. Create a synthetic training set of graph path questions from the Freebase schema used by WebQSP, with verbalized relation chains and gold logical forms. Compare three systems: (1) standard fine-tuning on WebQSP only baseline, (2) synthetic-pretrain then WebQSP fine-tuning, (3) retrieval-augmented fine-tuning baseline following a ChatKBQA-style setup. Evaluate Exact Match and Hit@1 on WebQSP test, with separate reporting on compositional vs single-relation subsets.

scope_conditions.method: fine-tuning with synthetic graph-structured supervision before or alongside task SFT
scope_conditions.task: domain-QA over knowledge bases or structured domain corpora

evidence_gap: Existing evidence supports synthetic-data gains in reasoning and some domain settings separately, but not a clean cross-cluster experiment showing synthetic reasoning curricula improve domain-QA composition.

hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies that work for reasoning could transfer to domain-QA, matching or exceeding full fine-tuning when the domain shift is narrow, but underperform when retrieval integration is the main bottleneck.
mechanism: Reasoning results suggest LoRA/PEFT can target the most task-relevant submodules with far fewer trainable parameters; in domain-QA this may preserve base knowledge while adapting answer style and evidence use, unless the task chiefly depends on external retrieval calibration rather than parametric adaptation.
predictions: LoRA matches full SFT on PubMedQA within 1 F1 point.
LoRA underperforms RAG-tuned models on retrieval-heavy domain-QA.
minimal_test: Fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct on PubMedQA and BioASQ using four conditions: (1) no fine-tuning baseline, (2) full supervised fine-tuning, (3) LoRA fine-tuning on attention and MLP layers, (4) LoRA plus RAG. Compare against the full-SFT and RAG baselines using Accuracy on PubMedQA and macro-F1 on BioASQ factoid/list questions; also report trainable-parameter count and inference latency.

scope_conditions.method: parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA/PEFT, optionally combined with retrieval
scope_conditions.task: domain-QA with moderate domain shift and available supervised labels

evidence_gap: The literature cited here shows PEFT gains on reasoning and some domain-QA success separately, but lacks a targeted test of whether PEFT transfers as well as full SFT across domain-QA regimes with and without retrieval.

hypothesis: Intermediate-step supervision from fine-tuned multi-step reasoning models could be repurposed as a learned rollout evaluator for search-based reasoning, improving search accuracy while pruning false-positive branches.
mechanism: Fine-tuning methods that explicitly teach intermediate reasoning structure may produce a verifier/value signal over partial chains; using that signal inside tree or breadth-first search could bias expansion toward semantically valid next steps and away from superficially plausible but incorrect branches.
predictions: Verifier-guided search beats unguided search on StepGame accuracy.
False-positive intermediate chains decrease relative to vanilla TSE.
minimal_test: Train a step-level verifier on GraphSolver+ style intermediate reasoning traces from the graph reasoning tasks in arxiv:2403.04483v4, then plug the verifier in as the node scoring function inside Thought Space Explorer on StepGame. Compare against vanilla TSE and direct decoding on StepGame; report final answer Accuracy and intermediate-step error rate / false-positive-chain rate.

scope_conditions.method: search methods with explicit partial-chain scoring such as TSE or reward-guided search
scope_conditions.task: symbolic or graph-like multi-step reasoning where intermediate traces can be labeled

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the payload shows a fine-tuned step-supervision signal being transferred into search-time branch evaluation on the same or related reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Synthetic curriculum data that benefits fine-tuning on compositional or graph reasoning could also improve search-based reasoning if used to warm-start proposal policies, especially on smaller models.
mechanism: Fine-tuning on synthetic graph/coding/compositional data may reshape the model's local next-step proposal distribution so that search explores higher-quality candidates earlier; this should matter most when the base model is small and search quality is bottlenecked by weak proposals.
predictions: Warm-started AR-MCTS yields larger gains on 7B/8B than larger backbones.
Search node expansions needed per solved item decrease after synthetic SFT warm-start.
minimal_test: Supervised-fine-tune Qwen2-VL-7B or LLaMA-3.1-8B on synthetic graph-based reasoning data derived from StepGame-style relational traces, then run AR-MCTS at inference on StepGame or a held-out graph reasoning benchmark. Compare against (a) the same AR-MCTS on the untuned base model and (b) SFT-only without AR-MCTS; report Accuracy and average search expansions/tokens per correct answer.

scope_conditions.method: search frameworks whose frontier quality depends on the model's proposal distribution, such as AR-MCTS
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning tasks with synthetic data generators and controllable compositional depth

evidence_gap: The payload contains separate evidence for synthetic-data fine-tuning gains and for search gains, but not for combining synthetic warm-start tuning with search in one controlled transfer study.

hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning targeted at reasoning modules could make search-based reasoning more compute-efficient than direct search on untuned models by reducing the breadth needed to reach correct solutions.
mechanism: If PEFT or LoRA sharpens latent reasoning transitions without full-model updates, then search algorithms that are breadth-sensitive may need fewer candidate branches to find correct paths, partially offsetting the token and time costs of search.
predictions: LoRA-plus-search reaches the same accuracy as base-search with lower token budget.
Breadth sensitivity decreases after PEFT, with smaller top-k maintaining accuracy.
minimal_test: Apply LoRA to a small reasoning model such as Llama-3.1-8B on a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset like GSM8K or LogiQA, then evaluate reward-guided search or breadth-controlled TSE with top-k in {2,4,8}. Compare against (a) untuned model with the same search and (b) LoRA model with direct decoding; report Accuracy, total generated tokens, and wall-clock time per problem.

scope_conditions.method: PEFT on models that can still expose candidate-step logits for search control
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning where search breadth and token cost are measurable

evidence_gap: Existing claims show PEFT can preserve or improve reasoning and that search cost depends on breadth, but there is no direct evidence that PEFT reduces the search budget required for a target accuracy.

hypothesis: Intermediate-step supervision that boosts fine-tuned multi-step reasoning models could make self-refine more reliable if those supervised traces are reused as explicit critique targets during refinement.
mechanism: Fine-tuning claims suggest gains come from exposing intermediate reasoning structure; converting that structure into a verifier-style refinement prompt may reduce the drift and answer-flipping seen in intrinsic self-correction by anchoring each revision to expected step-level invariants.
predictions: Step-labeled self-refine beats vanilla self-refine on GSM8K accuracy.
Answer-change rate drops relative to intrinsic self-correction.
minimal_test: Take Llama-2-7B from the self-refine instruction-tuning setup and run inference on GSM8K and MultiArith with two conditions: (1) baseline intrinsic self-refine prompt from the self-correction literature, (2) transferred step-anchored self-refine where the model must first align its draft to a small library of fine-tuning-style intermediate-step templates derived from GraphSolver+/RE-style explanation traces. Compare against standard prompting and vanilla self-refine using answer accuracy and answer-retention/change rate.

scope_conditions.method: transfer fine-tuning-style intermediate reasoning supervision into inference-time self-refine prompts
scope_conditions.task: textual multi-step reasoning with explicit chain-of-thought style decompositions

evidence_gap: No direct study in the payload tests whether step supervision that helps during fine-tuning can stabilize self-refine at inference time on the same reasoning benchmarks.

hypothesis: Synthetic curriculum data that improves fine-tuned graph and spatial reasoning could transfer to self-refine by supplying progressively harder self-generated revision tasks, yielding larger gains on high-hop problems than on easy instances.
mechanism: Fine-tuning results indicate synthetic and curriculum-like data help models internalize latent transition rules; using the same synthetic generators to create staged draft→critique→revise episodes may teach self-refine when and how to revise rather than merely asking for another answer.
predictions: High-hop StepGame accuracy improves more than low-hop accuracy.
Three-turn refinement degrades less when trained on curriculum-generated revision episodes.
minimal_test: Generate synthetic StepGame-style training episodes with hop counts 1-5 and convert each into self-refine tuples: initial incorrect or partial rationale, targeted feedback, revised rationale, final answer. Train a 7B open model with the R3V/self-refine recipe on these tuples, then evaluate on StepGame by hop count. Baselines: zero-shot self-correct prompting and self-refine training without curriculum ordering. Metrics: exact-match accuracy by hop and accuracy change from turn 1 to turn 3.

scope_conditions.method: curriculum self-refine training using synthetic graph/spatial reasoning episodes
scope_conditions.task: multi-hop graph or spatial reasoning where difficulty can be parameterized

evidence_gap: The payload shows synthetic data helps fine-tuning and self-training helps self-refine, but not whether synthetic curricula specifically improve iterative refinement stability on multi-hop reasoning.

hypothesis: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies that preserve reasoning quality with few trainable weights could make self-refine more sample-efficient if used to train only the critique/refinement submodule instead of the whole model.
mechanism: PEFT may isolate refinement behavior without overwriting base reasoning competence; this could avoid the regressions seen in some tuning and intrinsic self-correction settings while still learning a revision policy from self-refine data.
predictions: LoRA-refiner matches full self-refine tuning within 1-2 accuracy points.
LoRA-refiner preserves initial-answer accuracy better than full-model refinement tuning.
minimal_test: Use Llama-2-13B on GSM8K and CSQA with self-refine instruction-tuning data. Train three variants: (1) full self-refine instruction-tuning baseline, (2) LoRA only on attention/MLP layers used during refinement turns, (3) Q-Former-style narrow PEFT analogue applied only to a small critique head or adapter stack. Evaluate against standard instruction-tuned and vanilla self-refine prompting baselines using final-answer accuracy, first-pass accuracy preservation, and trainable-parameter count.

scope_conditions.method: parameter-efficient transfer of fine-tuning adapters into self-refine training
scope_conditions.task: reasoning benchmarks with supervised draft-feedback-revision examples

evidence_gap: Existing claims cover PEFT for fine-tuned reasoning and self-refine gains separately, but there is no direct evidence on whether PEFT is sufficient for learning iterative refinement policies without harming base reasoning.

hypothesis: Tool-use style hierarchical sub-question decomposition could improve search-based multi-step reasoning by making each search node correspond to an explicit, tool-like intermediate objective rather than a free-form thought.
mechanism: A fixed hierarchy of sub-questions can reduce branching noise and false-positive paths during search, aligning with claims that hierarchical tools offload reasoning burden and that breadth-first search quality depends on node usefulness.
predictions: Search with hierarchical sub-questions yields higher answer accuracy than vanilla search.
The gain is largest at small search budgets where branch quality matters most.
minimal_test: Implement a search variant of Thought Space Explorer or reward-guided search where each expansion is forced to generate a parent-labeled sub-question hierarchy before proposing child thoughts; evaluate on GSM8K and StrategyQA against the same search algorithm with standard free-form expansions, reporting exact-match accuracy and average tokens per solved example.

scope_conditions.method: hierarchical sub-question generation transferred from tool-use to search-based decoding
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning with limited search budget

evidence_gap: No direct experiment shows whether explicit tool-style hierarchy helps search node construction independently of adding external tools.

hypothesis: State-update ideas from tool-use pipelines could transfer to search-based reasoning by adding an explicit mutable reasoning state that is revised only when a search step produces verifiable new evidence.
mechanism: Like tool-use systems that update the working state only when a tool returns a meaningful output, search could gate state transitions to prevent hallucinated intermediate steps from contaminating downstream branches.
predictions: State-gated search reduces intermediate-step error rate versus ungated search.
Accuracy gains are larger on tasks with evidence accumulation than on short arithmetic tasks.
minimal_test: Augment AR-MCTS or TSE with a state-gating module: a child node updates the persistent reasoning context only if the model marks the step as evidence-producing and a verifier confirms entailment from prior context; test on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA against the same search algorithm without gating, measuring answer F1, supporting-fact F1, and percentage of invalid intermediate steps.

scope_conditions.method: verifiable state-update gating transferred from tool-use execution traces to search tree expansion
scope_conditions.task: knowledge-intensive multi-step reasoning with explicit evidence chains

evidence_gap: Existing search papers report better trajectories, but do not isolate whether selective state mutation rather than broader search is responsible.

hypothesis: Tool-use modularity could transfer to search-based reasoning by replacing monolithic backtracking with module-specific search operators, improving efficiency on hard reasoning tasks without full backtracking overhead.
mechanism: If different reasoning actions are modularized into operator types with separate expansion and rollback rules, search can prune or revisit only the failing module, potentially preserving the reliability benefits of modular tools while avoiding the time complexity of generic backtracking.
predictions: Operator-specific rollback matches or exceeds generic backtracking accuracy with fewer tokens.
The efficiency gain is strongest on hard multi-step tasks that currently trigger frequent search reversals.
minimal_test: Define three search operators for deduction tasks—decompose, infer, verify—and add operator-local rollback to a Tree-of-Thought-style or reward-guided search system; compare against identical search with generic global backtracking on Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects, reporting exact-match accuracy, wall-clock time, and tokens generated per problem.

scope_conditions.method: modular operator search with local rollback transferred from tool modularity
scope_conditions.task: hard symbolic multi-step reasoning where backtracking is common

evidence_gap: There is no head-to-head study testing whether tool-like modular operators can substitute for expensive generic backtracking in search-based reasoning.

hypothesis: Adding tool-style externalized verifier steps to self-refine will improve multi-step reasoning accuracy by turning refinement from unsupported introspection into grounded error checking.
mechanism: Tool-use methods appear to help by offloading subproblems to modular components and supplying extra evidence, while intrinsic self-correction often fails when the model only re-reads its own answer; a self-refine loop that must call a calculator, retriever, or grounding module before revising may reduce hallucinated edits.
predictions: Tool-augmented self-refine beats intrinsic self-refine on GSM8K.
Benefit is largest on arithmetic and retrieval-heavy subsets.
minimal_test: Implement a 2-round self-refine agent on GSM8K using GPT-3.5-Turbo or an open equivalent. In round 2, require the critic to emit executable checks via a calculator and Wikipedia retrieval tool before revising the answer. Compare against standard prompting and intrinsic self-correction from arxiv:2310.01798v2 on exact-match accuracy and revision success rate (fraction of initially wrong answers corrected without breaking initially correct ones).

scope_conditions.method: tool-grounded self-refine with explicit calculator/retrieval calls
scope_conditions.task: text-only multi-step reasoning, especially arithmetic and multi-hop QA

evidence_gap: No direct experiment in the payload tests whether external tools inside the self-refine loop, rather than standalone tool-use or standalone self-correction, causally improve refinement quality.

hypothesis: Transferring hierarchical task decomposition from tool-use to self-refine will stabilize multi-turn refinement by forcing local corrections on sub-questions instead of global answer rewrites.
mechanism: Claims about tool hierarchies and adjacent-node sub-question generation suggest that breaking reasoning into ordered micro-steps reduces cognitive load; self-refine failures may come from unconstrained whole-answer revision, so a decomposition-first refine policy could preserve correct earlier steps while editing only the faulty segment.
predictions: Step-local self-refine loses less accuracy over 3 turns than vanilla self-refine.
Error edits concentrate on one sub-step rather than rewriting all steps.
minimal_test: On GSM8K and HotpotQA, compare three agents with the same base model: standard prompting, vanilla 3-turn self-refine, and hierarchical self-refine that first decomposes each problem into numbered sub-questions, critiques each sub-answer separately, then only revises flagged steps before composing the final answer. Use exact match / answer accuracy plus a stability metric measuring accuracy after each turn and an edit-locality metric counting how many reasoning steps change per revision.

scope_conditions.method: hierarchical self-refine with explicit sub-question decomposition
scope_conditions.task: multi-step reasoning where intermediate textual steps can be enumerated

evidence_gap: The payload shows decomposition helps tool-use and that multi-turn self-correction can degrade, but it does not show whether decomposition alone can regularize self-refine without external supervision.

hypothesis: For multimodal reasoning, inserting a grounding-tool pass inside self-refine will selectively improve visual self-correction on perception-heavy benchmarks while leaving purely language-side corrections unchanged or slightly worse.
mechanism: Tool-use gains in visual reasoning seem to come from accessing additional grounded visual clues, whereas intrinsic self-correction in vision-language models is unstable; a refine stage that queries a grounding agent only when the critique detects object/text localization uncertainty could provide missing evidence instead of free-form reconsideration.
predictions: Grounded self-refine improves RealWorldQA over intrinsic self-correction.
Gains are larger on small-text and nuanced-object questions than generic visual QA.
minimal_test: Use MiniCPM-Llama3-V2.5 or Qwen-VL on RealWorldQA and SEEDBench. Add a self-refine variant where the critique may call a grounding module (for OCR/object crop extraction) before producing the revised answer; compare against initial generation and intrinsic self-correction VP-1/VP-3 baselines using accuracy, per-category accuracy on text-reading/object-detail items, and correction precision (share of revisions that improve the original answer).

scope_conditions.method: grounding-augmented self-refine with optional OCR/object-crop tool calls
scope_conditions.task: multimodal multi-step reasoning with perception bottlenecks

evidence_gap: Existing claims separately support grounding tools and self-refine for vision-language reasoning, but no cited work here tests a conditional grounding step nested inside refinement or identifies which visual error types benefit.

hypothesis: Retriever-aware RAG fine-tuning methods that help factual-QA will also improve domain-QA when the domain task depends on selecting small amounts of evidence, but gains will concentrate in retrieval-sensitive domains rather than structure-heavy semantic parsing.
mechanism: Fine-tuning both retriever and generator can increase evidence recall and reduce distractor exposure, which should transfer to domain-QA tasks with unstructured corpora; however, tasks whose bottleneck is logical form construction may see weaker gains.
predictions: PubMedQA EM rises over direct fine-tuning.
WebQSP gains are smaller than PubMedQA gains.

hypothesis: Applying reward-guided breadth-first search as an external verifier inside self-refine loops could convert unstable intrinsic self-correction into selective revision that improves multi-step reasoning accuracy.
mechanism: Search-based reward signals can act as an oracle-like critique filter, triggering refinement only when alternative reasoning branches score higher than the current chain, which may reduce the answer-retention and degradation problems seen in intrinsic self-correction.
predictions: Search-gated self-refine beats vanilla self-refine on GSM8K accuracy.
The gain is larger with breadth-3 search than depth-3 search at fixed token budget.

predictions: A self-refine model tuned on search trajectories exceeds one tuned on plain self-generated traces on MultiArith.
The tuned model makes fewer harmful revisions on initially correct GSM8K examples.
minimal_test: Create two instruction-tuning datasets for Llama-2-7B on GSM8K and MultiArith: one from search-based trajectory generation using Tree-of-Thought-style branching with reranking, and one from standard self-refine traces produced by single-chain draft-then-critique. predictions: Beam-refine improves RealWorldQA accuracy over 3-turn intrinsic self-correction.
Relative gains are larger on a smaller VLM than on GPT-4o-style stronger backbones.

hypothesis: The effect of chain-of-thought flips with dataset composition: CoT helps on multi-step or hard problems but can hurt or show little gain on short arithmetic or rationale-sensitivity benchmarks.

predictions: CoT gains grow with item step-count or difficulty.
On AddSub-like subsets, CoT advantage shrinks to zero or negative.

Template-controlled zero-shot runs show smaller or negative CoT gains.

Smaller models show more variance and more negative CoT cases.
